1, 2, 3, 4. In the spring of 1916 Imperial authorities suggested that recruiting be carried on in Canada for service in the British Navy. The British Admiralty sent Captain the Hon. Rupert Guinness to Canada in charge of a recruiting party. As it was not feasible to recruit for entry in the Royal Navy owing to the different rates of pay in the Imperial and Canadian services an agreement was arrived at between the Canadian Government and the British Admiralty whereby a division of the R.N.C.V.R. should be recruited for overseas service to form a part of the total forces that Canada proposed to put on active service in the war. maintopic: MAGDALEN ISLANDS AND PICTOU STEAMSHIP SERVICE.

speakeroldname: Hon. RODOLPHE LEMIEUX (Maison-neuve and Gaspe) moved:
maintopic: MAGDALEN ISLANDS AND PICTOU STEAMSHIP SERVICE.
speechtext:
For a copy of all correspondence, petitions and other papers concerning the steamer service between Magdalen Islands and Pictou, N.S.
He said: We are peculiarly situated in the county of Gaspe, which comprises the
peninsula on the Baie des Chaleurs and the river St. Lawrence and also the Magdalen Islands in the Gulf of St. Lawrence, about one hundred miles from the coast. The Magdalen Islands were, in former years, served by a steamer running between Pictou and the islands, touching en route at two or three ports of Prince Edward Island. Twenty years ago we had a weekly service, and I had that service changed into a semiweekly one. For many years we had an excellent steamer-I forget the name now,- for passengers, mails, and freight. At the beginning of the war the steamer was chartered by another company and was, I think, finally sold to the British Government. There is, on the Magdalen Islands, a very interesting fishing population, comprising about 7,000 people who are living and prospering there.. .Since the war began the service has unfortunately been exceedingly bad. I do not wish to blame the Government at all for the steamer service to the islands since the outbreak of the war, because the Government called for tenders and had to accept whatever boat was pffered. During the winter season, which begins generally around Christmas, and continues until the end of March or the beginning of April, there is no navigation between the mainland and the Magdalen Islands. It is, therefore, important that during the early spring, the summer months, and the fall of the year, there should be a regular service of the best kind for that population of 7,000 Canadians.
During the last four years it is regrettable, but it is not the fault of the Government, that the islanders have had practically no steamer service. A very small boat was put on the route, but it was not of sufficient capacity to transport the freight and the passengers. So much was that the case that I had to appeal every year to the Minister of Marine and Fisheries to be so good as to divert from its service the steamer Stanley, a good ice-breaker, or the steamer Laurentian. And I must offer my sincere thanks to the Minister of Marine and Fisheries who, last year and this year, was kind enough to send the Stanley and the Laurentian, much to the advantage of those islanders. During the last fall, on account of the influenza which broke out on the Magdalen Islands, the situation was very difficult and awkward. I, therefore, appealed to the Minister of Marine and Fisheries and he sent on board one of his steamers, doctors and nurses, and also a supply of medicine. Even during that time the regular service was maintained, but it is such a poor service that it is of no ad-

vantage at all to the islands. Many articles of consumption are imported into the Magdalen Islands from parts of Canada, chiefly from Nova Scotia, New Brunswick and Prince Edward Island. When there is a poor steamer service, as there has been during the last four years, the Government must rush to their rescue, and during the two or three weeks before Christmas, the Stanley or the Laurentian has to make several hurried trips, and even then at times, on account of weather conditions, the goods cannot be landed. Therefore, having conferred with the leaders on the islands, I have come to the conclusion that it is time for the Government to give to the islanders a steamer sendee controlled by the Government themselves. I do not believe in privately-owned steamers. A large subsidy is paid for the carriage of the mails, and there is general dissatisfaction as to the way in which those private owners conduct the service. That has been the case during the twenty years I have had the honour to represent the islands. I would ask the Government to treat the Magdalen islands, with their population of 7,000 people, as they treat Prince Edward Island. There is a regular service between Prince Edward Island and New Brunswick, and the Government could 'well afford to put a steamer on the route between Pictou and Magdalen Islands.
I have not the figures before me, but the islanders are great producers in this sense that they are splendid fishermen, and the best fish of the Dominion comes 3 p.m. from Magdalen Islands. The Government should take into consideration the fact that during several months of the year the islands have no communication whatsoever with the mainland, and, during the season of navigation the best service should be given to those taxpayers. I appeal to the acting Minister of Marine and Fisheries (Mr. Maclean) again to put the Stanley or the Laurentian on the route, because I have received from the warden of the county, Mr. Gaudet, a telegram which I have referred to the deputy minister. On the 8th of March last, this telegram was sent to me:
Have wired O'Hara-
The Deputy Minister of Trade and Commerce.

to-day as follows referring' yours fourth instant. Delay in collecting freight was caused by goods having been landed at different points of these islands other than their intended desti-ation and the difficulties of communication from one island to another at that particular season. The goods have not yet all been delivered, but people are paying their freight in the regular 
manner as they get delivery of their goods. I can definitely state this to be true as I am the freight agent at Amherst Island notwithstanding any report you may have received. The trip of the Stanley is urgently required and there would be no justification for your department to refuse sending her for reason quoted. Therefore our request being so much needed we hope to have a prompt and favourable answer. Please use every effort to have Stanley sent down.
(Sgd) A. J. Gaudet,
Warden.
I have received ten such telegrams from the different merchants and business men of the Islands. Surely, it is not fair to exclude these seven thousand people from the favours of the Government. They should have good and frequent communication with the mainland, as early as possible in the spring. We are unable to get an ice-breaker for the Islands, as the Stanley is in the Government service. I trust that the Government will do for the people of Magdalen Islands what they are doing for the people on the north shore below Quebec. I spend the summer at Murray Bay every year, travelling by the Intercolonial to Riviere Quelle; and from there an excellent service is provided by the steamer Champlain which plies between the north and the south the whole year round. I think it would be an easy matter for the Government to put one of their best steamers on the service between Pictou and the Magdalen Islands. I would again urge upon the Acting Minister of Marine and Fisheries the absolute necessity of sending the steamer Stanley at the earliest possible moment to carry the goods which were left last fall on the wharves at Pictou, and to distribute the freight among the different ports of the Islands.

maintopic: MAGDALEN ISLANDS AND PICTOU STEAMSHIP SERVICE.
speechtext:
I am interested in this particular service, as it touches two ports in my riding. It is a very important service, as a considerable amount of business is done on this route, particularly between Prince Edward Island and the Magdalen Islands, and between Pictou and Prince Edward Island. Prior to the war there was an excellent steamer on this route, but during the war the Government have not been able to provide us with a suitable boat. Last year the Enterprise, a small steamer which had formerly plied between Pictou, Georgetown, and Murray Harbour, was put on this route, but she was too small for the service. The Government also sent the Stanley in winter time, and She certainly did wonderful work. I am glad the hon. member for Maisonneuve

(Mr. Lemieux) has brought this matter up, and I trust the Government will provide the people of the Islands this year with a suitable boat large enough for the business. There are ports other than those of the Magdalen Islands which would be served by such a steamer. The service is of very great importance, indeed.
Hon. Mr. MACLEAN- I am sorry I am not at the moment in possession of such facts as would enable me to inform the mover of the resolution (Mr. Lemieux) as to the probable service that will be provided this season between Pictou and the Magdalen Islands. Of course, no objection whatever can be taken to his statement that this is an important route. During the war the subsidized coastal steamship services have been very much demoralized, and it has been impossible to keep them up to normal. I trust, however, that in the near future the services will be restored to something like their pre-war standard. There is generally considerable difficulty in the spring and fall of the year in securing suitable boats to carry to the Magdalen Islands the freight required at those7 particular seasons. It is also true that a great deal of the difficulty is due to the fact that the merchants of the Magdalen Islands postpone until a very late date getting in their goods; but I suppose there may be a very good answer to that from their standpoint.
Let me say on behalf of the Department of Trade and Commerce that we are very heartily in sympathy with the observations made by the mover of the resolution, and we shall do everything possible to give a proper service between Pictou and the Islands. I shall be very glad to confer with the hon. member privately with respect to this matter. I know that there has been a request for the steamer Stanley or some similar boat to convey certain goods from the mainland of Nova Scotia to the Magdalen Islands, the goods consisting chiefly of fishermen's supplies which will be required for their fishing operations in the course of the next few weeks. The Department of Marine and Fisheries and the Department of Trade and Commerce are doing everything possible to meet this request of the people of the Magdalen Islands. I assure my hon. friend we shall give -this matter constant attention, and if at all possible this request will be complied with.

maintopic: MAGDALEN ISLANDS AND PICTOU STEAMSHIP SERVICE.
speechtext:
I must thank the minister for his sympathetic hearing of my 40
request. The Islanders, as I stated a moment ago, are very grateful for what the department has done during the last two or three years. For the present I shall content myself with urging upon my hon, friend the necessity of providing a boat early this month to relieve the present situation. Will the department or the Government also consider favourably the suggestion I have made that in order to obviate difficulties in tire future they undertake that service themselves, as they do between Prince Edward Island and the mainland. I think that would be the only satisfactory thing to do for that population.

maintopic: MAGDALEN ISLANDS AND PICTOU STEAMSHIP SERVICE.
speechtext: I think there is a great deal to say in favour of the suggestion of my hon. friend and between now and the time when the Supplementary Estimates are before the House possibly I may have an opportunity to give fuller consideration to the suggestion.
Motion agreed to.

On motion of Hon. Arthur Meighen (Minister of the Interior), the House went into Committee on the following proposed resolution, Mr. Boivin in the Chair:
That it is expedient, to make provisions respecting advances for the purchase of seed grain, and to provide, on such terms and conditions as may be agreed on with any bank advancing moneys for the purchase of seed grain, that a guarantee by the Crown may be given to the said bank for the payment of the principal sum of such advances and interest

thereon at five i>er centum per annum; and that upon payment of the principal sum, or any part thereof remaining unpaid, the security held by the bank shall be endorsed to the Minister; and further, to prescribe the nature of the security to be taken for loans, the rate of interest thereon and date of payment thereof, the form of application for loans, and the officials to whom application is to be made and by whom the application shall he verified and approved, the commission to he paid to the banks, and such other provisions as may be necessary for the better securing of the advances.
We should have a very full explanation from the minister of the necessity for this action on the part of the Government and the steps that they propose to take in connection with it.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, hitherto, and for many years, the Department of the Interior has advanced moneys which were essential in necessitous cases to the holders of unpatented lands for seed grain purposes. In each case they have taken security on the unpatented land which was still in their possession; that is to say, on the Government title which the entrant had not yet earned. In the year 1915 the Dominion Government was compelled to extend its activity in seed grain distribution to the holders of patented lands as well taking in that case the same security upon the title under the authority of the provincial legislature. When the subject had to be attacked for the year 1919, it was my desire that the Government of Canada should confine its responsibility to unpatented lands only and that the responsibility for providing seed with regard to patented lands should resit upon the local or provincial authorities. At a conference of the representatives of the Governments affected an arrangement to that end was made. Thereupon, we being concerned only with unpatented lands, it occurred to us that a better arrangement could be made by co-operation with the banks for the distribution of this seed grain and particularly for the collection of the returns, than under the system which had hitherto prevailed whereby we advanced the money ourselves and took the means and the responsibility of collection. Consequently an Order in Council was put through ratifying an agreement which was to the effect that wherever seed grain was necessary on unpatented lands, the homesteader would make application to the agent of Dominion Lands within whose district his homestead lay. The agent of Dominion Lands, if necessary, would send a homestead inspector to ascertain the facts. If it was not deemed necessary he would certify without such in-
vestigation. Upon his certificate being presented to the bank as to the amount required and the character of each grade, certifying such requisites as the form prescribed, the bank was authorized to advance to the homesteader the money and take his note and a seed grain lien in accordance with the Bank Act as security therefor. The Government guaranteed the bank that the money so advanced would he returned with interest at five per cent. The note itself, and the lien, bore interest at seven per cent which amount the bank were authorized to collect and which they had the security for. The arrangement also provided that in so far as the bank collected, they would receive one per cent on the amount collected; consequently, when the bank collect, they get eight per cent. Where the bank does not collect it gets five per cent. This is an arrangement resulting in a very considerable inducement to the bank to collect the money. It eliminates from the Interior Department the rather expensive mechanism by which we have endeavoured in the past to collect these advances. Of course as yet, it cannot be said to have been fully tried out, but we hope that it will result in much better collections and at much less cost to the country. The resolution authorizes legislation looking to the implementing of the Order in Council passed and the provision of such machinery for the future on a permanent basis.

I think that the minister explained that the Government have the right to take over the security given and he said that the security would he in the form of a note and a lien taken under the Bank Act on the seed grain. The Government take a lien on the land, do they not? The banks cannot take a lien on the land? Therefore, the Government are dropping that portion of the security that they otherwise had.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: No, the land is unpatented land; consequently, we hold the land as security just as before if we take it over.

I think it is necessary that there should be some limitation of the amount. This appears to give a blank cheque to the Government, or to grant authority to advance for this purpose an unlimited sum. It may be that there is something in the preceding legislation to limit the outlay of the Government. I only draw the minister's attention to it. This is am authority to pay or guarantee money and there must be some limitation to the amount.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
I do not think the previous legislation is different in that respect.
I have not the exact terms of that legislation in my mind, but it enables the Government to advance money on unpatented land. Necessarily, we will have to have a vote of Parliament to pay the amount. The amount advanced in each case must be limited as it is only to be for the seed, certified by the agent of Dominion Lands, required for a man's homestead and not for any other purpose.

Last year the hon. Minister of Railways and Canals (Mr. Reid) brought in legislation asking for an unlimited amount for railway equipment. The amount was not mentioned and when the question was raised by the hon. member for Shelburne and Queens (Mr. Fielding) he withdrew Iris resolution and came back with a stated amount.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
This is very different.
One might estimate what would be required to acquire a railway.

It was for railway
equipment.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: Whatever the case may have been, hut we do not know what amount will be required to provide seed grain in any particular spring. It all depends on the conditions of the previous year and the condition of the farmers in any district. It has varied from year to year. I do not presume there has been anything like uniformity. I know there has not been. We have had to advance amounts beginning with almost nothing and running up to $12,000,000.

Cannot you suggest an
average?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
The average would
be $5,000,000 but I would never suggest to Parliament that it would amount to $5,000,000 in any one year. I do not think the amount can he suggested.

The wording here is:
" Any part thereof remaining unpaid." How long .a time are the hanks authorized to loan for?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
The notes all fall due
on or before the first of January.

In the succeeding year?
40i

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: In the succeeding year and the bank has a certain time, unless it is extended by the minister, within which to call upon the department for payment. If the bank calls upon the department for payment, it then gets five per cent.

My recollection is that when we embarked upon the policy of advancing money for the purchase of seed grain to western farmers we were told that it was to be temporary and only to meet an emergency. It seems now to be renewed eveiy year. I would like to know what view my hon. friend takes of the matter. Is it intended that this shall be a permanent advance, year afteT year, or is it only for a limited time?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
The first question my hon. friend raises has reference to the advance of 1915, which was on a wholly different basis from any other advance. That was on patented and unpatented lands, and reached a total of between twelve and thirteen million dollars. Every year for I do not know how many years-I have no doubt for thirty-advances have been made on unpatented lands-that is on our own lands -to homesteaders, and that is all this legislation contemplates. Consequently there is no change at all. As to the second question, namely, that relating to repayments, I can answer that in so far as the large advance of 1915 was concerned. We have met with very considerable delay and not wholly satisfactory results in repayment. The sanguine hopes of many have not been met,
' and at the same time the pessimistic expectations of others have been surpassed. Of that $12,000,000, I think I am safe in saying, we have received between eight and eight and a half millions; it is not below that figure, it may possibly by this time have come up to about $9,000,000. That money, however, was not wholly advanced for seed grain-I will give the exact figures to the House at any time-it was advanced, to the extent of I think about five millions, for relief, the other seven millions being for seed grain. The relief money has been the most difficult to collect. All the security we were able to get was a lien on the land, over and above all registered liens at that time, therefore the difficulty in collecting. The lessons we have learned as the result oi our experience in connection with seed grain liens has resulted in my decision to try this experiment.
Is it the intention of my hon. friend to continue the payment of 3 per cent for the collection as formerly?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: There is no rate of 3 per cent, and there never has been.
I understood my hon. friend to mention 5 per cent and that 3 per cent was collected in addition to that.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: All that the farmer pays is 7 per cent, no matter to whom he pays. If he did not pay the bank the bank calls upon the department, and the department collects 7 per cent from the farmer.
The Government only pays 5 per cent to the bank?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: The department guarantees 5 per cent to the bank, and for what it collects the bank receives 1 per cent.

Is there any intention on the part of the department to handle seed grain throughout the country? For instance, the Department of Agriculture has a commission buying and handling seed grain. Has that any relation to the policy now under discussion?
IMr. MEIGHEN: No. The commission in connection with the Department of Agriculture-I know something of its operations, as I was Acting Minister of Agriculture for a time-has to do with the selection of seed grain and its distribution for cash to municipalities and others. It has nothing to do with the distribution of seed grain to homesteaders on liens. It simply selects, tests and issues when the seed grain from a germinating standpoint is good, and sells that seed grain at the price paid for it-sells for cash.
Or less?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: On the only occasion of which I am able to speak definitely, on account of the rise in the price of grain, the department came out very considerably ahead, although that was not intended.

I think the objection of the member for Queens and Shelburne is worthy of some consideration, and might be met by the minister making an estimate of what he expects will be required in the coming season. There is no doubt this matter should be brought before Parliament from year to year, and the amount voted which is expected to be required or to be guaranteed. It seems to me that the present system is rather loose. In the first place, the Government is a very poor collector at any time. The inducement of the bank is not very great and its responsibility is nothing at all; the bank simply lends the money and is guaranteed 5 per cent in any event, the same as if it were making advances to
[iMr. Murphy.]	'
the Government. I think the bank should be made responsible in some way and assume some share of the responsibility if it is being guaranteed the money. It has a chance to make 8 per cent if it looks after the collections, but it gets 5 per cent in any event. I think it would be better if the bank were made responsible for the collection of this money. It will not sue any person under this arrangement, and there is no provision for it; it simply hands over the security when it gets tired of the arrangement to the Dominion Government, and leaves it to the latter to collect. If the Government were to guarantee the bank 80 per cent of the advances made, and stipulate that there should be no interest paid on what it did not collect, it would have some chance of getting a little better security and loaning it to a better class of people. If this were limited to the homesteader it might not involve so much money, but there is nothing in this regarding unpatented lands. A friendly immigration agent would manage to get a good deal of money at 7 per cent invested in Canada at the present time. If the banks loan money, and are not saddled with any greater responsibility than is here provided and can hand their securities over to the Dominion Government for it to take action at some future time, it seems to me such loans would be pretty easy for the banks to make, and the fellow who gets the money is not in any worse position but in a much better position than ever before.
May I ask the minister if he can give us any idea of the losses which have been incurred by the Government in connection with those advances? ,

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
There is virtually no loss with respect to advances on unpatented lands, because in every case we have the land, and if the homesteader abandons it the seed grain lien is charged against it and must be paid by the next entrant. I know I am safe in saying that there is no need for consideration on the part of the House of the iquestion of loss so far as our past history is concerned. There will be losses in connection with relief and seed grain advances on patented lands, particularly with relation to relief. Personally, I am very confident that loss will amount to a very small proportion, and even if we lost a substantial share of the sum that was advanced in 1915 the investment on the part of Canada would well have been an excellent one because the results to this country were pretty nearly in the Scriptural proportion of a hundred fold. I would like to meet the

point raised by the hon. member for Queens and Shelburne, if I could see any.way of doing so, although that was not what was really discussed by the hon. member for Pontiac. I do not see any way to do so for this reason: Presuming we were to fix a figure, say of $1,000,000, and when the spring came that amount would not provide seed, thousands of acres of land are going to go unseeded, or else we would simply have to take the money by Governor General's warrant; we could not do anything else, we could not possibly stand by and see the land go unseeded. Therefore no very great object would be gained by fixing an amount for such a peculiar cause as this. However, if the resolution passes I will give further thought to the question, and when the Bill is before the House there will be an opportunity for an amendment to that effect.
Resolution reported, read the first and second times, and concurred in.

speechtext:

On section 1-definition:

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: This is merely to take care of the case of one stream meeting another and the intention of the Act that no claim shall extend over 500 feet. Further, the special meaning attaching to "base line" in mine surveying is given.

Virtually, it asserted its control over the power to divert water within the area covered by the Act. The Act just covers a certain defined area in western Canada. Clause 1 of this Bill makes the following provision:

No person shall divert or use any water from, and no person shall construct or cause to be constructed any dam or other works for the impounding- of water in any river, stream, watercourse, creek, spring, ravine, canyon, lagoon, swamp, marsh, or other body of water, otherwise than under the provisions of this Act, except in the exercise of a legal right existing at the time of such diversion or use or construction.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General

speechtext:
Did we not, at the last session, make a permanent extension of credit to the banks, or something similar to this? 5	p.m. ing money cheaper and commodities dearer.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
I think my hon. friend must have reference to action taken to continue the provisions of the Finance Act in operation last year. The Finance Act, as I pointed out, contains provisions which can be invoked only in time of war or real or apprehended financial panic. The proclamations which have been issued and the action taken so far would come to an end with the official conclusion of the war. The result is we should be where we were before the war broke out in 1914. For the reasons that I have mentioned, the general unsettled financial conditions of the world and the necessity of conserving gold reserves, it is undesirable that we should revert to that condition. We, therefore, ask that the measures which have been so effectual during the war-and they have been exceedingly effectual and in the national interest-should be continued for a period not exceeding two years after the war, subject to being terminated by Order in Council at such time as we think they are no longer necessary. 1 think it is undoubtedly in the national interest that this legislation should be passed.
My hon. friend speaks of fiat money. I have no hesitation in saying that of all the belligerents that have been in the war since the beginning, the financial position of Canada is undoubtedly the best. There is no question about that. The United States, as I pointed out, was in the war for nearly two years. The position of the United

States with regard to its circulation is as I have indicated, but I do not believe it is more favourable than that of Canada in that respect.
My hon. friend has asked with regard to the regulations against the export of gold from Canada. Those regulations are still in effect, and will be continued in effect so long as we think it necessary to protect the gold reserves of the country. At the present time gold would be shipped to Asia or to other parts of the world where it might be in demand, for the purpose of building up gold reserves, and it is very necessary, by reason of the expansion of note issues in Great Britain, the United States, and this country that gold should be conserved. Generally speaking, with regard to restrictions and regulations, it has been the policy and is the policy of the Government to cancel them just as rapidly as in our judgment the national interests of the country will permit. Almost immediately upon the declaration of the armistice we removed the restrictions against issues in our market by provincial and municipal governments. A little later we removed all restrictions upon issues, when the Government no longer needed the market, and when it was clear that those issues would be made without any detriment to the national interest. I can assure my hon. friend that no one desires more keenly than I do to get rid of all restrictions imposed by Order in Council, and I am sure that would be the view of other ministers, because one effect of these Orders in Council is to increase our administrative duties. With regard to gold and silver, for instance, applications are made for license to export, and these applications have to be considered and decisions given upon them. My happiness as a minister will be greatly increased when all restrictions are removed. There is no object in the Government keeping in force any Order in Council a day beyond the time it is actually needed in the national interest. I realize, of course, there may be a difference of opinion as to just when an Order in Council should be cancelled, but the Government must exercise its discretion with regard to that having in view the national interest as it sees it at the time.

The hon. member for Pontiac seems to be under the impression that the facilities of the banks for issuing circulation are being increased .by this legislation. I do not understand it to be so. What I understand is that the emer-
gency provisions ought to be extended for a period after the war, and, speaking generally, in view of the very uncertain conditions prevailing and the large business enterprises that will have to be carried out in the reconstruction period, I think it is well that the power of the Government to assist the banks in that way-it is not a new power-should be extended for a reasonable time after the war. Did I hear my hon. friend read, amongst the securities against which we issue Canadian notes, Canadian treasury bills?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Yes, but not owned by the Dominion of Canada; owned, let us say, by a bank.
Issued by the Dominion Government, and coming back to us as the property of others?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Yes.

Otherwise, it would be tantamount to a man putting his own note in the safe and thinking he was richer. With regard to the fifteen per cent excess circulation, the origin of that goes back some years, I think to 1907, when there was a very disturbed financial condition in the United States, and for a while it seemed as if we would have a very disturbed financial condition in Canada, particularly in the West The banks were largely restricting their credits, business men were becoming very much alarmed, and altogether the situation was very dangerous At that time, the Government of tbe day took upon themselves-straining their authority, I admit-to issue excess circulation, not bank circulation, but Dominion circulation, and to loan it to the banks if they wished to have it to meet the demands of the occasion, particularly with regard to the moving of the crop in Canada. My recollection is that the amount authorized to be issued, if you call it authority, was $10,000,000, and of that I think little more than half was actually issued. It was another case of the old lady who heard the bank where she deposited her money was in trouble and went to the bank and asked for her money, and when it was given to her, said: " Now I know you have it, I don't want it." When it was known that the Government of the day had the facilities and were willing to help the banks, the banks themselves loosened up and there was no need to issue the full amount proposed by the Government. Of course, it was a straining of authority, and at the following session of Parliament legislation had to be introduced

to authorize and indemnify those who were concerned in the issue of those notes. But out of that experience wisdom was learned. We learned that while our arrangements for circulation as between the Government and the banks were satisfactory for ordinary business, in the case of stress or emergency there was need of some greater power, and the result was that at the following session an Act was passed to provide for what might for convenience be called emergency circulation. In that case it was proposed that the circulation should be issued by the hanks. In the actual transaction that had taken place just previously the circulation was issued by the Government. It was proposed that the banks during a certain period of the year,-the crop period,-should he allowed, in addition to their ordinary powers of circulation, to issue excess circulation to the extent of fifteen per cent of their combined paid-up capital and rest. That worked out, I think, very well. Some bankers at the beginning did not like it. I remember one very eminent banker who said that no self-respecting bank would ever use it, but I think his own bank saw fit to use it afterwards. I understand that the Finance Minister is proposing to continue for two years after the war that scheme, which was only intended in the first place to meet the emergency of the crop season. I think it is very desirable that the extension should not be made for a longer period than is absolutely necessary, but I do think the minister is wise in keeping this power in his hands in view of the very disturbed financial conditions which may reach us in the reconstruction period.

I should like to call the attention of the Minister of Finance to the fact that the American Government are trying to gather in all the gold they can. Not long ago I had the experience of taking some gold across into the United States, and at the border the gold was taken from me, as it is from everybody else, and American bank notes were given in exchange for it. The security may be just as good, but the object of the American Government is to strengthen their note issue by gathering in gold from every one who is passing into or out of their country. I do not see any effort of that kind being made in Canada, though possibly Americans are bringing across gold to this country and taking it over to Europe with them. There are no doubt many of our people who are holding a certain amount of gold, perhaps two or three hundred dollars, which in the aggregate would amount to quite a lot if we
gathered it in to strengthen our gold reserve as the Americans are doing.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
I am interested in what my hon. friend has said. Perhaps I should inform the committee as to the gold holdings of the banks, before the resolution passes. I have pointed out that the gold holdings of the Dominion have increased from $97,000,000 in July, 1914, to $121,000,000 at the end of January of this year; an increase of $24,000,000. The gold held by Canadian banks has also been substantially increased. In July, 1914, it amounted to $54,000,000 roughly speaking. On January 31st, 1919, it amounted to $91,000,000, an increase of $37,000,000. So that we have come through the war, both the banks and the Dominion Government, with a very substantial increase in the gold reserves which we hold.

maintopic: RECLAMATION OF DOMINION LANDS BY DRAINAGE.

speechtext: Hon. ARTHUR MEIGHEN (Minister of Interior) moved the second reading of Bill No. 9 to authorize the reclamation of Dominion Lands by drainage.

maintopic: RECLAMATION OF DOMINION LANDS BY DRAINAGE.
speechtext: 'Before the Bill is read a second time, perhaps the minister will explain whether he thinks it desirable in view of the large quantities of land which we are supposed to have in this country, to go to any very great expense for reclaiming land. Perhaps the minister would explain whether this is going to be an expensive process or whether it is desirable, in view of the very large tracts of land which we have, to go to any large expense in reclaiming swamp lands.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
maintopic: RECLAMATION OF DOMINION LANDS BY DRAINAGE.
speechtext:
It is not the purpose of the department to go into the reclaiming of swamp lands on an extensive scale; at all events, at first. I do think it desirable though that we should commence now to do some work in the way of reclaiming our reclaimable lands that are not at present in
use by reason of their water content. The area of our land available for farming purposes while great is not so great as the terms in which we have been accustomed to speak of it. The amount of land found available, or immediately suitable, for Soldiers' Settlement is indeed rather disappointing. But aside from the question as to the amount of land available the country should, in so far as it is our duty, as distinguished from the duty of the provincial authorities, endeavour to reclaim and make available for cultivation any lands of this character that can be economically dealt with in this way. Very often they are situated in districts whose development is retarded simply by reason of the fact that these swamp lands are there and that the duty of reclaiming them, on whomsoever it may rest, has not been undertaken.
The United States of America has, through its Secretary of the Interior, Mr. Lane, thrown out a very large programme as being under contemplation at least by that Government. We do not contemplate a programme as extensive as that contained in the manifesto of Mr. Secretary Lane. The way this Bill comes to be introduced is this: We have constitutionally, and we have asserted it, by our Irrigation Act, passed many years ago, control of the surface water and that control we have exercised in Alberta, Saskatchewan and the added portion of Manitoba. While we had that control, the control of drainage and the whole jurisdiction as to drainage were in the hands of the provincial authorities. As a consequence of that dual 'control the development of the country through drainage has been held up in the districts in which the Crown lands were ours. I may say as a premise, now, that the cardinal principle that I keep before me in this discussion i,s that our duty in regard to drainage arises by virtue of our ownership of the Crown lands.
Under those circumstances certain conferences were held before I was Minister of the Interior, between the authorities of the three Prairie Provinces and the Dominion, with a view to arriving at a division of responsibilities with respect to the various classes of drainage projects between the provincial governments and the Dominion Government. As a result of those conferences the drainage projects were divided into four separate classes. I might denominate those classes as follows: First of all, small drainage projects involving an expenditure not exceeding $2,000-merely

the drainage of say small lakes. The second were a class covered within the scope of a drainage project by a provincial government looking to the construction of highways- such drainage work as was necessary in its highways programme-and which drainage affected Dominion lands and could not he done unless provision was made either for a charge against the Dominion lands, *or for some other arrangement that would get over the difficulty. The third class were those that were on a scale that should best be taken care of under the drainage district laws of the province-not under the highway laws, hut under the laws which provided for the establishment of drainage districts, in which, of course, the Dominion had certain lands. The fourth class were those in which the Dominion owned the great area of the lands, and consequently upon the Dominion would be the great body of responsibility. A division of duty was arranged between the provinces and the Dominion with regard to those four distinct classes, and certain legislation became necessary, both on the part of the provinces and on the part of the Dominion, to carry out the arrangements agreed upon as the result of the conferences. The province of Alberta responded to its duty in this respect by the passing of its Reclamation Act in April, 1917. The province of Saskatchewan took similar action in, I think, December of the same year, and also by certain amendments to its Highways Act. The province of Manitoba has not yet acted, but its Government has now appointed a drainage commission whose duty it will be to report on this as on other drainage matters. The Government of the Dominion, on its part, first of all provisionally accepted the arrangement by an Order in Council, and then last session passed legislation amending the Dominion Lands Act so as to enable sales of Dominion lands to be made to the provinces for the purpose of embracing those lands within drainage schemes, and thereafter selling such Dominion lands on certain terms. That legislation was in accordance with the arrangement arrived at as to the disposition of the second and third classes of drainage projects that I have just described. All that now remains for us to do, in order to carry out the full intent of the agreement arrived at, is to pass legislation to enable the Dominion to assume its responsibility with respect to that class of drainage projects where we initiate and carry out the enterprise-that is to say, in those cases where the great area of lands is ours, and consequently where the great benefit is ours. What is necessary is to 
enable us to come in, just as a private person or as a district \*)uld, and operate under the drainage laws of the provinces of Alberta and Saskatchewan-and Manitoba also when the requisite legislation has been enacted-and to reelaim land thereunder. That is the purpose of this Bill. I may also say that provision is made for assessments against privately owned lands tha't come within the purview of any scheme of reclamation we may undertake-assessments against them for their share of the cost of the undertaking-and likewise provision whereby we can take advantage of the provincial laws that look to the maintenance of the works after they are completed.

maintopic: RECLAMATION OF DOMINION LANDS BY DRAINAGE.
speechtext: I should judge from the explanation of the minister that the purpose of this Act is to secure land for the purpose of settlement,-to some extent, at any rate,-by returned soldiers, and farmers as well?

speechtext: That enters into the object, although I do not wish to hold it out as the immediate object, because land for settlement cannot be very quickly got by reclamation measures. It will take some time for this to become fit land for settlement.

speechtext: That is the very point upon which I desire to get information. Some time ago I read an editorial in the Globe which gave some figures purporting to have been used by Premier Martin in connection with land settlement relating more particularly to the soldiers, and, as far as I can recall the premier's statements, there were available in the surveyed area of the Dominion only about twenty-three million acres of land.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
maintopic: RECLAMATION OF DOMINION LANDS BY DRAINAGE.
speechtext: Available where?

maintopic: RECLAMATION OF DOMINION LANDS BY DRAINAGE.
speechtext:
That there were only about twenty-three million acres of land available in the surveyed area of public lands. Premier Alartin went on to point out that of over 200,000,000 acres of surveyed land, so much was granted to railways, 8,000,000 acres were covered by water, 5,000,000 acres were under grazing leases, and so'on. I can see, as the minister says, that any reclamation scheme of drainage is going to be very slow in its operation. I would therefore ask him if any policy is to be adopted by his department whereby lands can be reclaimed more quickly. I understand that certain representations were recently made to him, as head of the department interested, under which lands would be reclaimed for the purpose of settlement by the soldiers in

a much more rapid way, by taking areas that had been burned by forest fires, or in other ways, and which settlers would not like to take up at present on account of the unclean condition in which the land was left. I understand it was pointed out to the minister that by the department adopting a scientific system, and at the proper time of the year, these areas, which are very extensive, could be very rapidly reclaimed and made available for settlement by soldiers and farmers. I presume that this Bill does not cover that sort of reclamation at all. Therefore I would like to know if any steps are being taken by the department over which he presides along the lines suggested by the Dominion land surveyors.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
maintopic: RECLAMATION OF DOMINION LANDS BY DRAINAGE.
speechtext:
The hon. gentleman is right in his view that this Bill does not contemplate that class of reclamation. That subject, however, has been under consideration. There are areas of land that have been burned over that, in the opinion of many who should be in a position to judge, can be more quickly and expeditiously made available for actual and immediate settlement by means of a system of burning. But there is a difference of opinion as to that. I may frankly say there is a difference of opinion among the officers of the department as to the wisdom of undertaking such an experiment. I know of no method that has been suggested except a re-burning, and there are scientific methods of doing that. Against those who say that it can be done at this season of the year,-because we are now approaching the season when that should be done if it is going to be undertaken,-it is argued, and argued very strenuously, that on account of the nature of the material that will be deposited on the ground,-that is now deposited there, and would be deposited in greater quantities by a system of slashing,-but heat produced by burning would consume or remove material, and so would affect the value of the soil for farming purposes.
As between the two schools of opinion 1 have not come to a conclusion. I do not like to launch upon an experiment of that kind unless I feel the ground very safe beneath me, and I do not feel it safe just jet. There may be differences of opinion between members of the House on this subject, and I am sure that there are other members whose views based on experience, would be more valuable than mine.

The conference took
place only between the Governments of the three Prairie Provinces and the Federal Government, I am disposed to think that the same principles could scarcely be made to apply to British Columbia. speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
maintopic: THE PRIVILEGES OF THE HOUSE OF COMMONS.
speechtext:
I beg to draw the attention of the House to the following Address of the Senate, which was delivered to me during the recent recess:
That an humble Address be presented to His Excellency the Governor General, praying that His Excellency will cause to be laid upon the table of the Senate a return of copies of all papers, letters, telegrams, memorials, petitions or other communications or documents in the possession of the Government or in that of His Honour the Speaker of the House of Commons, which may be available, in connection with the recent delegation from the farmers of Canada to present certain public and national questions and issues to the attention of the Cabinet and of the Parliament of Canada.
It appears to me that this Address constitutes a breach of the privileges of this House, and that if it is obeyed without protest it might be treated as a precedent that would in the future be a source of inconvenience and embarrassment. I would point out that the authorities on parliamentary procedure are all agreed that where one House of Parliament desires communi-catioh of any papers or documents belonging to the other the proper course is to send a message asking to be supplied with the papers in question (see Bourinot, 4th edition, pp. 281, 282; May, 12th edition, p. 563). This practice, too, has, as far as I can ascertain, been invariably followed in all similar communications between the Houses. I beg to submit, therefore, for the consideration of the House, whether it would not be proper to send a message to the Senate drawing attention to the Address, pointing out the uniform practice that has hitherto existed between the two Houses, and stating that the Address, being a breach of a very important privilege of

the House, might, if unobjected to, form a dangerous and objectionable precedent.

speakeroldname: Mr. D. D. McKENZIE (Cape Breton North):
maintopic: THE PRIVILEGES OF THE HOUSE OF COMMONS.
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it has been my privilege to see a copy of the decision which you have submitted to the consideration of the House, and I may say at once that I fully concur in the conclusions which you have reached in respect to the order which was passed by the honourable the Senate. It is, of course, of the highest importance that each Chamber should maintain its full and absolute autonomy, and that there should he no encroachment whatever by one body upon the rights, privileges, powers and immunities of the other. It is also equally true that nothing in the way of obstruction should exist which would prevent the members of either branch of the Parliament of Canada froni obtaining the fullest possible information respecting any public matter. If that object can be attained-and I think it can-without any infringement of the rights of either, and without the creation of any friction between the two great bodies which govern the country, it is of course proper and well that the ends sought to be attained should he reached without difficulty, and that there should be no clash between the two Houses. As the practice in the past has furnished ample provisions for the obtaining of such

information, and as there is no precedent for refusing any request that has hitherto been made by the Senate upon this body, or by this body upon the Senate, there is no reason to believe that anything but the greatest possible harmony will exist in future in regard to the supplying of such information. And I know that the Government and the officials of this House and yourself, Sir, will always meet any reasonable and proper demands that shall he made for such information as may be sought by the Senate. Knowing that the machinery in existence, and the constitution and rules which have been recognized hitherto have been ample for such purpose, I think it would be well to stand by these old rules; and I am of the opinion that your decision. Sir, is proper and constitutional, fully conserving the rights and dignities of this Chamber.

Mr. S. W. JACOBS (George Etienne Cartier) moved for leave to introduce Bill No. 26, to amend the House of Commons Act.
Explain.

Mr. Speaker, this Bill is designed to correct an abuse which has existed for many years in this country, whereby the Government in power can keep an electoral seat vacant as long as it suits its purpose. Unfortunately, this abuse cannot be attributed entirely to the present Government because Governments that have preceded it have been equally guilty. It is proposed by this Bill that within sixty days after a seat is declared vacant a new writ shall issue for an election. The rule in England is exactly in line with this. As many hon. members know, within a remarkably ghort period after a seat is declared vacant, I think it is three weeks in England, the writ issues for a new election. By this Bill it is proposed that sixty days shall be allowed before the election takes place. Because of geographical conditions we cannot very well fall in line with England and prescribe a similar term; otherwise I would have moved to introduce the same law, as to the delays.
Another provision of the Bill is that no member of Parliament may sit for more than one seat. There is a standing order of the House that no member shall sit for more than one seat, but, as Bourinot remarks, it is a rule that is honoured more in the breach than in the observance. This Bill proposes to make a statutory enactment that no member may sit for more than one seat, and that if he persists in doing so, he shall incur a penalty of $200 a day. It is provided further that he is not to make election, or declare his option, until the delays for protesting his seat have expired, because, without such a provision, a member might escape an investigation into the manner in which the election was carried on. After the delays have expired for protesting the seat, the member must declare his option in order to escape the penalties mentioned in the Bill. I am sure that the'Bill will appeal to the good sense of the House, and I hope to see it carried.

Motion agreed to and Bill read the first time.

Canadians, members of the Canadian Expeditionary Force, seconded to the Royal Air Force, are awarded War Service Badges in the same manner and under the same regulations as members of the C.E.F.
Canadians who are not members of the Canadian Expeditionary Force but who joined the Royal Air Force directly are not, under the present regulations, eligible for Canadian War Service Badges. They are eligible for badges issued by the Imperial authorities.
The question of issue of Canadian War Service Badges to Canadian citizens whose service has been exclusively with the Imperial Forces has received extended consideration. There were a number of objections to issue of Canadian badges to soldiers whose services was not with the Canadian farces; the principal one being that no record of service of such soldier is available at Militia Headquarters.
These difficulties have, however, been met, and an Order in Council which provides among other things for award of Canadian badges to those Canadians who resided in Canada on August 4, 1914, and who served in the Imperial Forces and have returned to take up their residence in Canada, has been prepared and is expected to he passed shortly.

speechtext:
I desire to read the following message from the Overseas Minister of Militia (Sir Edward Kemp):
Following are some of the things provided for entertainment and occupation of troops whilst awaiting embarkation.
General training. Upon cessation of hostilities it was immediately decided to eliminate the more particularly offensive training from the syllabus. Maintenance of health of troops and their preparation for demobilization became (Paramount thought. Syllabus has been laid down for daily physical training, discipline, ceremonial parades and route marches to limited extent. Remainder of time has been taken up in instruction by Khaki University of Canada in all areas and sports and athletics with object of maintaining health and contentment of troops as far as possible and fitting them for their civil duties.
Education. A concentration camp in connection with the work of Khaki University has been opened at Ripon for the purpose of assembling and giving instruction In more advanced educational work to suitable students. Establishment of this camp has proved very popular, and keen competition has been apparent to gain admittance. At present there are in session between 750 and 800 students. Approval has been given for attachment of officers and other ranks who have studied for at least two years at a University in Canada prior to enlistment, to enable them to continue

m
their studies. This privilege has been extended to some 300 students with creditable service overseas. Total attachment to date 307. Battalion schools organized for men seeking elementary education comprise elementary agriculture and commercial arithmetic, etc., area colleges in each area for men to study who have studied higher matriculation, etc. At concentration camp, Ripon, matriculation first and second years arts, applied science and first year pre-medical studies is given. Men attached to British Universities who require third and fourth year work in graduated studies.
Literature is distributed amongst Canadian troops, such as Booklet number 2, information regarding land settlement and agriculture. Copies Canadian Government pamphlet entitled " Canada and her soldiers," have been despatched to France for distribution to Canadian troops.
Athletics. Teams selected from Canadian personnel in England and France will compete in International events in England during spring and summer of this year, embracing boxing, pushball, baseball, soccer, football, lawn-tennis, and athletics; field and track events. Sub-committees have been formed for each sport comprising officers and other ranks. Canadian boxing championship, O.M. F.C. in British Isles was held at Witley on February 27, before a very enthusiastic audience. Sum of five thousand dollars has been authorized from a special fund in connection with expenses incurred in training of Canadian teams buying surplus sporting equipment, extra messing where necessary. Sunday travelling expenses, etc.
Activities of Canadian Y.M.C.A. An officer has been placed in charge of athletic work in interests of Y.M.C.A. and prepared to co-operate fully in matters of athletic programmes. Distribution of boxing gloves and footballs, etc., has been made to all Canadian areas. Complete list of sport equipment it is expected will be required to carry out extensive athletic programme contemplated during coming summer; has been prepared to cover wants of Canadian troops in British Isles. In each area there are from four to six Y.M.C.A. huts which are supplied with concert parties, luxuries, cinemas, table games and free stationery. There are also canteens in each area selling various goods such as cleaning kits, etc., etc., at cheapest rates. Pamphlets on citizenship have been distributed among troops numbering approximately fifty thousand copies. During the year 1918 the sum of sixty-eight thousand dollars was expended out of Y.M.C.A. fund in purchasing equipment for troops in England, total comprising England and France amounted to one hundred and sixty-four thousand dollars.
In London a Leave Bureau has been established to take care of Canadian soldiers in England on leave who have no homes on this side. Man is put up for six days in London, including bed, meals, tour every day of city, four theatres and comforts of private home twice during this period for two pounds, five shillings or eleven dollars. About twenty thousand men per month pass through Leave Bureau. Free coffee bars are established in England at points at which troops arrive from France, where they are supplied with free coffee and food. On board ships a Y.M.C.A. officer is supplied to each conducting staff. He has with him magic lanterns and slides for entertainment purposes, gramophones, tables, games, athletic material, writing paper, etc., and organized entertainment on board.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
That the House do go into Committee to consider the following proposed resolution:
Resolved, That it is expedient to bring in a measure to ratify and confirm,-
(1) The Order in Council of the seventh day of March, 1919, which provides as follows:

"Whereas under the authority of "The Appropriation Act No. 2, 1918," the Governor in Council advanced the sum of $7,471,399.93 or thereabouts to the Grand Trunk Pacific Railway Company for certain purposes in said Act defined, including the meeting of "deficit in operation of the Grand Trunk Pacific Railway System," such sum being in addition to other large sums previously advanced under previous authority for similar purposes.
"And whereas a letter dated 4th March, 1919, from the Vice President of said Company was received by the Minister of Finance, as follows:-
"I am instructed to inform the Government that in view of the fact that the increased rates applicable to the Grand Trunk Pacific Railway have not been sufficient to meet the increased operating expenses, dt will not -be possible for that Company to continue its operations when the present funds have been exhausted, which will be about 10th instant. May I ask you to be so good as to acknowledge receipt of this letter."
"And whereas should the operation of the Grand Trunk Pacific Railway System be discontinued, great detriment to the public interests would ensue, and the intention of Parliament in authorizing the said advances would be defeated.
"And whereas the continued operation of said system is essential in the present position of Canada resulting from the war, which has not yet been terminated by Peace, especially in connection with the transport of returning Canadian Troops and of supplies and equipment and freight, and other services made necessary . by the war.
"And whereas for the protection of the public interests and for the purposes aforesaid, it is essential that the operation of said system should be continued without interruption.
"And whereas the duty of continuing such operation is thrown upon the Government of Canada inasmuch as there are no effective provisions in existing laws whereby such continued operation could be otherwise secured.
"And whereas immediate action by the Government is imperative.
"Therefore, His Excellency the Governor General in Council, under the authority of the War Measures Act, 1914, and of all other authority in that behalf, is pleased to order and it is hereby ordered as follows:-

"1. In this Order, unless the context otherwise requires:-
"(a) 'Grand Trunk Pacific Railway System' means and includes (1) the lines of railway and their appurtenances and the undertaking and works of the Grand Trunk Pacific Railway Company, of the Grand Trunk Pacific Branch Lines Company and of the Grand Trunk Pacific Saskatchewan Railway Company, (2) the lines of telegraph and their appurtenances and the undertaking and works of the Grand Trunk Pacific Telegraph Company, (3) the steamships, vessels and their appurtenances and the undertaking and works of the Grand Trunk Pacific Steamships Company, (4) the properties, hotels, and appurtenances and the undertaking and works of the Grand Trunk Pacific Development Company.
"(b) 'Officers' means and includes Directors, President, Vice-Presidents, Managers, Secretary, Treasurer, Clerks, Servants and employees.
"(c) 'Books and papers' means and includes books of accounts or of entries relating to the business or operation or maintenance of the said lines of railway or telegraph or steamships, vessels, hotels, properties or works, or any of them, or any part thereof, also* records, statements and documents relating to such business, operation, or maintenance or any part thereof.
"(d) 'Exchequer Court' means the Exchequer Court of Canada.
"(e) The singular number includes the plural and the plural the singular, the male gender includes the female, and the female the male.
"(f) * Person ' includes corporation.
"(g) 'Government Receiver' means the Receiver appointed by this Order.
"2. The Minister of Railways and Canals is hereby appointed Receiver of the Grand Trunk Pacific Railway System, and such Receiver shall have and exercise with respect to the said system and every part thereof and to the companies included therein, powers and duties similar to those of a receiver under Section 26 of the Exchequer Court Act.
"3. On the application of the Government Receiver the Exchequer Court of Canada may make such orders respecting such Receiver and his powers and duties and the carrying out thereof including the issue of Receiver's Certificates, as the Court may deem necessary or expedient in the public interest.
"4. Subsections 5 and 6 of section 26 of the said Act shall apply to the Government Receiver and to the Grand Trunk Pacific Railway System and every part thereof and to the companies included therein-except that no remuneration of the Receiver shall be fixed by the Court.
"5. The Government Receiver may, on or after the 10th day of March, 1919, or on such earlier day as the Grand Trunk Pacific Railway Company, or any Company included in the Grand Trunk Pacific System, may cease to operate efficiently its undertaking and works, or any portion thereof, take possession of such undertaking and works, and the Exchequer Court may from time to time make and enforce such orders in aid of the Government Receiver with respect to taking of such possession or otherwise as the Court may deem expedient for carrying out of the provisions of this Order according to their true spirit and meaning.
"6. Each Company included in the Grand Trunk Pacific Railway System and its officers shall facilitate the carrying out of the powers and duties of the Government Receiver, and all books and papers, real or personal property

of each of the said Companies, in its possession or under its control or the control of its officers or any of them, shall without delay be handed over to the said Receiver or his nominees or placed under his control in such manner as he may direct.
"7. Any officer of the Company included in the Grand Trunk Pacific Railway System, who obstructs the Government Receiver in carrying out his powers and duties, or fails to hand over to him or his nominees, or to place under his control, any book or paper, real or personal property in accordance with the foregoing provisions, shall incur a penalty for each breach of said provisions of the amount hereinafter stated, viz., in the case of a President, a VicePresident or a Director, the sum of Ten Thousand Dollars ($10,000) ; in the case of a Manager, with the authority of or similar to that of a General Manager or of one acting for or assisting a General Manager, the sum of Five Thousand Dollars ($5,000) ; in the case of a Secretary or of a Treasurer, or of one acting for or assisting a Secretary or Treasurer, the sum of Two Thousand Five Hundred Dollars ($2,500) ; in the case of any clerks, servant or employee, the sum of One Thousand Dollars ($1,000).
"8. Any penalty incurred under the foregoing provisions may be sued for and recovered, with costs, in the Exchequer Court, by suit or proceeding in such Court instituted by the Attorney General of Canada.
"9. Nothing in this Order contained, and nothing done or to be done under the authority hereof, shall render the Government of Canada or the Government Receiver, or any one acting under the authority of the Government Receiver, or of the Exchequer Court, liable to the Grand Trunk Railway Company of Canada, or to any Company included in the Grand Trunk Pacific Railway System, or to any creditor, or holder of any bonds, debentures, debenture stock or other securities of the said Companies or any of them, for any claim by reason of the making of this Order, or of anything done or to be done under the authority hereof, or under the authority of the Government Receiver or of the Exchequer Court, nor shall afford any defence to, nor shall prejudice any claim, action, or proceeding of the Government of Canada which the Government might lawfully make or take had this Order not been made.
" 10. All Officers except the Board of Directors of any Company included in The Grand Trunk Pacific Railway System shall continue to discharge for the Government Receiver, till further orders or directions by him, duties in connection with the operation and management of the undertakings and works of any Company included in The Grand Trunk Pacific Railway System, similar to their present duties, so that no interruption in the operation and management thereof may occur.
"11. Nothing herein contained or done, or to be done hereunder shall prejudice the exercise by the Exchequer Court or by any Court of any Province of Canada of its present jurisdiction under the Exchequer Court Act, or under any other law of jurisdiction to appoint a receiver or to order or decree a sale or foreclosure of any railway, or section thereof, or other property affected by this Order; provided that before any such sale or foreclosure is ordered or decreed or any Receiver is appointed by any such Court, notice of the application shall be given to the Minister of Railways and

Canals of Canada, and he, or counsel for him, shall be heard upon the application ; and the Court in granting, or refusing or postponing the application, shall take into consideration the public interests involved, and shall make such order as shall in the opinion of the Court protect the public interests.
"12. The Minister of Railways and Canals mentioned in this Order means the Minister for the time being, and upon a vacancy occurring his successor shall become the Government Receiver. The powers and duties of the Government Receiver may be exercised by such member of the Government as may from time to time be the Acting Minister of Railways and Canals.
"13. Should it be made to appear to the Government Receiver that any book or paper is or has been used for the purposes of the operations of the Grand Trunk Railway Company of Canada, as well as the operations of any company included in the Grand Trunk Pacific Railway system, and that for such reason the same should not be handed over to the Receiver or placed under his exclusive control, the Government Receiver may, on such terms and condition as he may deem necessary, allow the joint use of same to be continued. The Government Receiver may open such books and accounts as in his opinion may be necessary, to separate and transfer from any such book or paper, jointly used, accounts and entries relating to any of the companies included in the Grand Trunk Pacific Railway System, and may so separate and. transfer the same; and the said Receiver shall keep the accounts of his receipts, expenses and disbursements in connection with each of the companies included in the said System and their works, undertakings and properties, or parts thereof, in such manner that one may be distinguished from another, and that the interests of the various parties interested therein may be ascertained.
"14. The Governor in Council may, from time to time, under the Order of the Exchequer Court, and upon the security of Receiver's Certificates, or otherwise, advance to the Government Receiver such sums as may be required to enable him to exercise his powers, and to perform his duties as Receiver; the sums so advanced shall be paid out of any unappropriated moneys in the Consolidated Revenue Fund of Canada.
"15. No transfer of any shares in the Capital Stock of any company included in the Grand Trunk Pacific Railway System shall, after the appointment of the Government Receiver, be made, and no such transfer shall be entered on any register or transfer book. Any transfer contrary to this provision shall be null and void; provided that the Government Receiver may, on the application of any person interested. or of his own motion, permit any transfer to be made or completed."
