speechtext: Motion agreed to, and the House went into committee on the resolution, Mr. Boivin in the Chair.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
The request of my hon. friend the leader of the Opposition for correspondence or other information relating to this resolution, and the Bill to be founded upon it, is reasonable, and before the Bill is introduced we shall be glad to produce such correspondence as we may find which is relevant to the proper consideration of this question.
With regard to the agreement to which he has referred, namely, that which was entered into in 1903 between the Grand Trunk Pacific Railway Company and the Government of Canada, bon. members will find that agreement in the statutes of 1903, chapter 71, an Act respecting the construction of a National Transcontinental Railway. The agreement which had been entered into is found in a schedule to that Act. In 1904, further legislation was introduced into Parliament validating an amended agreement, and making further provisions with reference to the transaction. Therefore, such members of the House as may desire to familiarize themselves with the legislation, and with the agreements between the Grand Trunk Railway Company and the Government of Canada, will find all necessary information in the statutes of those years.
It had been my intention, on consideration of this resolution to give a brief resume of the Grand Trunk Pacific Railway transaction, and to furnish to the committee a considerable part of the information for which my hon. friend has properly asked.
In 1903 an agreement was entered into between the Grand Trunk Pacific Railway Company and the Government of Canada for the building of what is known as the National Transcontinental Railway. That National Transcontinental Railway embraced two divisions: the Eastern division from Moncton to Winnipeg, and the Western division from Winnipeg to Prince Rupert. The Eastern division was built by the Government of Canada upon plans and [DOT]specifications agreeable to the Grand Trunk Pacific, and was built through a commission. The intention was that when that Eastern division from Moncton to Winnipeg was completed, it should be leased by the Grand Trunk Pacific Railway Company, [DOT]which was to construct, own and operate the Western division, that is to say, the main line from Winnipeg to Prince Rupert and the subsidiary undertakings. The Grand Trunk Pacific Railway Company was to lease the Eastern division from Moncton ito Winnipeg for seven years, and was to pay no rent, but only the operating expenses. After a period of seven years it was to pay three per cent on the cost of construction of the Eastern division of the National Transcontinental Railway, the lease being for a period of fifty years altogether.
With respect to the Western division of the National Transcontinental railway, the construction of the line was to be financed by the sale of bonds guaranteed by the Government of Canada and by the sale of bonds guaranteed by the Grand Trunk Railway Company; and here I may say that the proprietary interest of the Grand Trunk Pacific Railway Company, which was to own and operate the Eastern division, and lease that division, was in the Grand Trunk Railway Company of Canada. The Grand Trunk Railway Company of Canada was to own all the stock, and does as a matter of fact own all the stock, of the Grand Trunk Pacific Railway Company. So that the Grand Trunk Pacific Railway Company, and indeed the entire National Transcontinental railway, became a part of the Grand Trunk Railway Company's system. The Western division was, as I have said, to be financed by the sale of securities of the Grand Trunk Pacific Railway Company, guaranteed by the Dominion Government, and guaranteed by the Grand Trunk Railway Company of Canada. The Dominion Government was to guarantee bonds of the Prairie Section (which, roughly speaking, extended from Winnipeg to Edmonton) to an amount not exceeding 313,000 per mile.
The Dominion Government was to guarantee the securities of the Grand Trunk Pacific Railway Company required to construct the Mountain Section, extending roughly, from Edmonton or thereabouts to Prince Rupert, to an extent of three-quarters of the entire cost of that Mountain Section. The Dominion Government was given first charge upon the undertaking from Winnipeg to Prince Rupert, the bonds of the Grand Trunk Pacific Railway Company which I have referred to, guaranteed by the Dominion, being secured by trust mortgage covering the enterprise. Next after that charge came the securities of the

Grand Trunk Pacific Railway Company guaranteed by the Grand Trunk Railway Company of Canada, to an amount of about 520,000,000. The House will, therefore, readily grasp the plan of finance which was to ensure the construction of the National Transcontinental railway. Just let me summarize.
The Dominion Government was to build the Eastern division from Moncton to Winnipeg. With respect to the Western division, the Dominion Government was ^ to guarantee bonds of the Grand Trunk Pacific secured by first mortgage. The Grand Trunk Railway Company of Canada was to guarantee second mortgage bonds of ibe Grand Trunk Pacific Railway Company, and it was thought at the time that the proceeds of bonds so guaranteed would be adequate to construct the Western division. As it transpired, the proceeds of the bonds mentioned were not sufficient, and in 19o9 legislation was introduced into Parliament whereby the Dominion Government made an advance of $10,000,000 to the Grand Trunk Pacific Railway Company upon the guarantee of the Grand Trunk Railway Company of Canada. The proceeds of that loan were found not sufficient, and in 1913 a further loan of $15,000,000 was made by the Government of Canada to the Grand Trunk Pacific Railway Company upon tne guarantee of the Grand Trunk Railway Company of Canada. The proceeds of that loan were found not sufficient to complete the enterprise and here a departure took place. The Grand Trunk Railway Company, which, as I have stated to the House, has a proprietary interest in the Grand Trunk Pacific Kailway Company, declined to guarantee any further loans made by the Government to the Grand Trunk Pacific Railway Company for the purpose of its completion. It was put forward that the finances of the Grand Trunk Railway Company would not permit the Grand Trunk Railway Company to increase its guarantees of loans made by the Government to the Grand Trunk Pacific Railway Company. It was considered desirable in the national interest, and having regard to the fact that the enterprise had been carried on so far, that the undertaking should be finished, and a further loan made by the Government. And in 1914 a loan of $16,000,000 was made by the Government of Canada to the Grand Trunk Pacific Railway Company, such loan not being guaranteed, as had been the case with the two previous loans, by the Grand Trunk Railway Company of Canada. The proceeds of that last loan were adequate to complete 
the line, which was finished at the end of 1915.
The position then was that the Grand Trunk Pacific Railway Company had completed its enterprise by the financing which I have mentioned. The Grand Trunk Railway Company of Canada owned, and still owns, all the stock of the Grand Trunk Pacific Railway Company. The Grand Trunk Railway Company then, through its president, notified the Prime Minister that the Grand Trunk Railway Company, to use his own terms, had " come to the end of its tether," as far as the Grand Trunk Pacific Railway Company was concerned. In 1916, in order to provide for the payment of interest upon securities of the Grand Trunk Pacific Railway Company, and to provide for deficit in operating expenses-because there has been, with the exception of one year, a continuous deficit in operating expenses on the Grand Trunk Pacific Railway Company,-the Government voted in the Estimates the sum of $8,000,000. That was in 1916.
Now, I desire to point out to the House that the Dominion Government, since the original agreement was entered into, and without being obliged to do so under the terms of the original agreement, in 1909 made a loan of $10,000,000, guaranteed by the Grand Trunk Railway Company; in
1913	made a loan of $15,000,000 guaranteed by the Grand Trunk Railway Company; in
1914	made a loan of $16,000,000 direct to the Grand Trunk Pacific Railway Company; and in 1916 Parliament voted $8,000,000 for the purpose of providing for the interest upon the securities of the Grand Trunk Pacific Railway Company,- guaranteed not only by the Dominion Government but by the Grand Trunk Railway Company of Canada,-and, further, to meet deficit in operation expenses, the Grand Trunk Railway Company of Canada taking the view that they should not be called upon to furnish any money for the operation of that railway company. In 1917, the situation continuing as it was, Parliament again voted the sum of $7,500,000 for the same purposes. Of that sum about $5,000,000 was expended. Last year Parliament again, at the instance of the Government, voted the sum of _ $7,500.000 for the same purposes.
Were these loans or gifts?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
These three I have last mentioned were loans-$8,000,000 in 1916; $7,500,000 in 1917, of which $5,000,000 was paid out, and $7,500,000 voted last year.

These were loans to the Grand Trunk Pacific Railway Company secured by blanket mortgage upon their enterprise.
Were these advances also made on the expectation of the Grand Trunk being able to carry out its original agreement with Canada?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
The Government has never expected any thing else than that the Grand Trunk Railway Company of Canada would carry out the bargain which it entered into with the Government of Canada. At the same time, the present Government of Canada, like the Government which preceded it, has been desirous of assisting in the completion of the enterprise and adopting a generous attitude not only towards the Grand Trunk Pacific undertaking but towards the Grand Trunk Railway Company of Canada itself; the Grand Trunk being a pioneer company whose operations have meant much to this country.
Mr. LEM.TEUX: Was the interest always paid?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: The interest was always paid but it was paid from the money which Parliament voted. Parliament voted the money which paid interest upon the Grand Trunk Pacific securities, guaranteed by the Dominion Government and guaranteed by the Grand Trunk, and paid also the deficit in the operating expenses. The interest has been paid only because the Dominion Government, over and above any obligation which they had under the agreement, have provided all the money for the purpose.
Was this $8,000,000, $7,500,000 and $7,500,000 guaranteed by the Grand Trunk?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
No, it was a direct loan to the Grand Trunk Pacific, not guaranteed by the Grand Trunk Railway Company, but secured by a blanket mortgage on the entire enterprise. The Grand Trunk Pacific Railway Company has not been able to pay its fixed charges with the exception of one year, and then only to a small extent. There has also been a deficit in operating expenses, which is to-day and will be for the coming year a larger amount than it was last year.
In order that the committee may understand the attitude of the Grand Trunk Railway Company of Canada towards its obligations with respect to the Grand Trunk Pacific, I desire to refer to what is known as the Drayton-Acworth report. The Government saw the railway situation developing in a way that required attention and action, and in 1916 they appointed a commission to look into the entire railway situation of Canada and make such recommendations as they thought proper respecting the transcontinental railway systems. That commission consisted of Sir Henry Drayton, chairman of the Board of Railway Commissioners, Mr. Acworth, an eminent London financier and railway authority and Mr. Smith, President of the New York Central Railway System. They made a report, Mr. Smith dissenting from the conclusions of his colleagues.
The Drayton-Acworth report has been before the House and is available to any member who may desire to read it. To those who take an interest in the railway situation in Canada and especially those who want to know something about the rr>blem before us, I cannot too earnestly commend this report of Sir Henry Drayton and Mr. Acworth in respect to the Grand Trunk and the Grand Trunk Pacific Railway situation. The report deals, amongst other things, with the question of the Grand Trunk Railway Company and with that of the Grand Trunk Pacific Railway, which, as I have stated, is a subsidiary of the Grand Trunk Railway Company. At page 26 the report calls attention to the fact that the chairman of the Grand Trunk Railway, writing to the Prime Minister, states "they are at the end of their tether," and that "it is quite impossible for them to meet the extra liabilities arising from the Grand Trunk Pacific Company." That is to say that Mr. Smithers, who is the chairman of the Board of Directors of the Grand Trunk Pacific Railway Company, wrote to the Prime Minister, as I stated a little while ago, to the effect that they were at the end of their tether and that it would be impossible for them to meet the extra liabilities arising from the Grand Trunk Pacific Company. What these liabilities are, I shall explain to the House in a moment. At page 26 of the report I find a statement expressing the opinion of the commissioners upon the Grand Trunk Railway Company of Canada towards their liability with respect to the Grand Trunk Pacific Railway Company. The commissioners say:
"We cannot think that this is a reasonable proposition, or one that we could advise the
Government to acoept

We think the Grand
Trunk Company cannot thus escape the consequence of its own action. We quite agree that the Grand Trunk Company cannot meet its Grand Trunk Pacific liabilities. But, if the Government is to relieve the Grand Trunk Company of liabilities which it voluntarily incurred.

but which it now finds impossible to meet, it is for the Government, not for the Company, to fix the terms."	*
To show further the attitude of the Grand Trunk Railway Company, I read from the report an extract from the examination of Mr. Chamberlin, who was president of .the Grand Trunk Pacific Railway Company and also of the Grand Trunk Railway Company:
Sir Henry Drayton-Doesn't it really come down to this thait the statements in your letter mean that in your view, in order to protect the finances of the Grand Trunk, and as a corollary to protect the finances of the country the Government ought to relieve the Grand Trunk itn regard to its investment; isn't that the whole thing?
Mr. Chamberlain-That is the whole thing.
Sir Henry Drayton-There is nothing else to it?
Mr. Chamberlain-Nothing else.
That clearly shows that the Grand Trunk Railway Company, proprietors of the Grand Trunk Pacific Railway System, had come to the conclusion that they would not continue to be responsible for the payment of the interest upon the securities of the Grand Trunk Pacific; that they would not be responsible for the deficit in its operations but would cast the entire burden of the Grand Trunk Pacific Railway Company upon the Government of Canada; in other words, wash their hands of the entire transaction.	,

Does the minister
think that the Grand Trunk Railway could by any ipse dixit, or action of their own, relieve themselves of their responsibility under the original agreement?

speechtext:
Thd Grand Trunk Railway. That is to say if the Dominion Government took over the Grand Trunk Railway of Canada, and strict regard was
had to its legal liabilities in respect of the Grand Trunk Pacific, the amount which should be paid by the Government in compensation to the shareholders would, in the language of the report, be very small.
Not paid by the Government, paid by the company.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
The Commissioners are discussing here the question of the Dominion Government taking over the Grand Trunk Railway of Canada, and they say that if regard should be had to the liabilities of the Grand Trunk Railway Company of Canada in respect of the Grand Trunk Pacific, the amount which the Government of Canada should be called upon to pay for that stock would be very small. But the Board of Commissioners took a rather generous view of the situation, as the Government of Canada has taken and is prepared to take of the situation. Neither the Commission nor the Government has ever had it in mind to deal harshly, to exact the pound of flesh, as the saying is, from the Grand Trunk Railway of Canada. Now let me read to the House what the Commissioners said on that point:
But we do not think this is the only basis on which the people of Canada should proceed. We think this is a case for generosity rather than strict justice. Canada is under obligations to the Grand Trunk shareholders, who, in the early days, with hut small Government assistance, and in competition with the railways of the United States, with their vastly greater resources, built up the first Canadian railway system. In, later times the Company has had further to meet the competition of heavily subsidized Canadian rivals, and it cannot be said that at any stage of its history the shareholders have obtained excessive profits on their enterprise. On the whole we recommend that on condition of the surrender, by the Grand Trunk Company of their entire share capital, guaranteed, preferred and ordinary, the trustees grant a certain annuity, charged as a working expense on the whole undertaking of the Dominion Railway Company, for the first seven years, increasing at the termination of that period by something like 40 or 50 per cent. We have left the figures blank, as there will he questions of cash in hand, value of stores, etc., which must make the precise figures subject to negotiation. But our meaning is that the first figure shauld be a moderate but substantial percentage of $3,600,000 (the average dividend payment for the last ten years).
The Commission say, from a strictly legal point the share capital, by reason of the liabilities of the Grand Trunk Railway Company toward the Grand Trunk Pacific Railway Company, has but very small value, but dealing with them generously they recommend that for the period of seven years there should be a moderate but substantial percentage of $3,600,000, in-

creasing at the termination of that period by something like 40 or 50 per cent.
In ordeT that the Committee may realize the financial interest which the people of Canada and the Grand Trunk had in that Grand Trunk Pacific enterprise, let me make a statement with respect to its financial position.
In any action which it is taking with regard to the railroads of this country, is the Government being guided by the Drayton-Acworth report?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
I stated at the time the Commission was created, when the same question was put by the former Minister of Railways (Hon. Mr. Graham), that it would be for the Government of Canada to exercise its discretion and judgment as to what policy would be followed. We appointed a Commission, but we did not give them plenary power to determine the policy of the Government. Nevertheless, the report is an exceedingly valuable one. In the three years which have passed since that Commission was created and in the two years since the report was made, I have come more and more to the conclusion that the Drayton-Acworth report is one of the most valuable reports that has ever been made upon railway matters in this country. I am perfectly satisfied, speaking for myself, that in the administration of railway enterprises which come under the control of the Dominion Gevernment, the machinery recommended by the Drayton-Acworth report will be utilized. In my opinion, it is the best for the purpose.
Now, I was going to show the financial position of the Grand Trunk Pacific. The figures are staggering. The members of the House are generally familiar with the situation, but the public do not understand it, and I am satisfied that the shareholders of the Grand Trunk Railway Company do not understand it. I do not believe that the shareholders of the Grand Trunk Railway Company have been made fully aware of the extent of the liabilities of the Grand Trunk Railway Company towards the Grand Trunk Pacific enterprise. 1 will give the figures slowly so that hon. gentlemen can dwell upon them, because they are very large indeed.
The Grand Trunk Pacific Railway Company-which has about 1,700 miles from Winnipeg to Prince Rupert and about 1,000 miles in the Grand Trunk branch lines system; and which has also its subsidiary Development company, owning lands, hotels, steamships and other assets-has outstanding securities guaranteed by the
'
Dominion Government to the extent of $84,000,000.

Who are the holders
of those securities?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
That $84,000,000 includes the securities, to which I made reference earlier in the course of my remarks, guaranteed by the Dominion Government and secured by a first mortgage upon the line from Winnipeg to Prince Rupert. It includes also a portion-I think, speaking from recollection, about $7,500,-000-of the $16,000,000 issue of 1914 guaranteed by the Dominion Government. But the $84,000,000 are bonds of the Grand Trunk Pacific bearing the guarantee of the Dominion of Canada.
My hon. friend asks who holds these securities. The Dominion of Canada holds $33,000,000 of them; they are in our vaults. We took them under what is known as the implementing agreement, which the Committee may recall; and instead of having them sold on the market at a low price, the Dominion Government took them at par. It is a good thing we did, because of the $84,000,000 outstanding we hold $33,000,000 ourselves. Nevertheless, they are outstanding; the money was advanced; the interest is payable; the legal liability on the part of the Grand Trunk Pacific exists precisely as if these securities were in the hands of holders in England, United States or Canada. The remainder of the securities are in the hands of bondholders in Great Britain principally; I think comparatively few of them are held in this country.
In addition to that $84,000,000 the Dominion Government made a loan of $10,000,000 in 1909 and another loan of $15,000,000 in 1913, a total of $25,000,000 guaranteed by the Grand Trunk Railway Company of Canada. One would think that that guarantee of the Grand Trunk Railway of Canada would be sufficient to relieve the Dominion Government from any anxiety with regard to the $25,000,000. But the Dominion is concerned in that $25,000,000, because it loaned the money, notwithstanding the fact it is guaranteed by the Grand Trunk Railway Company of Canada. I have mentioned the votes which were loans secured by mortgage-$8,000,000 in 1916, $7,500,000 in 1917, of which $5,000,000 were paid; and $7,500,000 in 1918, a total of about $20,000,000. So that the Dominion Government, on top of the figures I have mentioned, is interested to the extent of $20,000,000 further by reason of votes made by Parliament during the last three years.

In addition, the Grand Trunk Pacific lines in Alberta and Saskatchewan have issued ooiids to the extent of $13,000,000 guaranteed by Alberta and Saskatchewan. Just consider the amount of public credit that is involved there. $84,000,000, $25,000,000, $20,000,000-$130,000,000 represents the extent to which the Dominion Government is, by its guarantees or by the obligation of the Grand Trunk Pacific or the Grand Trunk Railway Company as guarantor, interested in the finance of this system.
Has the Minister not omitted to mention the $16,000,000 issue in 1914?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: My hon. friend is right; I have inadvertently omitted to mention that. If ycu add the $16,000,000 to the amount which I have mentioned, you get a total of $145,000,000 of interest which the Dominion Government has in. the Grand Trunk Pacific Company and in the guarantees which I have mentioned of the Grand Trunk Railway Company of Canada.
Is it the intention of the Government to take over the branch lines and pay the provinces-for the amounts guaranteed by them?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I will come to that a little later.
Suppose the guarantee or endorsement. of the Grand Trunk Railway Company is good; what is still our direct liability in respect of our own guarantees?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
That can easily be calculated. The Dominion Government would be liable as guarantor? in respect of $84,000,000, upon which the interest charged per annum would be about $2,400,000.
Those are, I think, the figures shown in the Drayton-Acworth report, but there must be added the interest on the loans made during the last three years for the purpose which I have mentioned, and the rate of interest being high, there would be a substantial increase-in round figures, I should say a total of $3,000,000 at least. In addition to the Dominion Guarantees in respect to this enterprise, I desire to place the committee in possession of information respecting the guarantees of the Grand Trunk Railway Company of Canada. The Grand Trunk Railway Company of Canada lias guaranteed securities of the Grand Trunk Pacific Railway Company to a total amount of $97,000,000.

That does not overlap the Dominion guarantees?
42}

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
No, it overlaps only the $25,000,000 I have mentioned. I will tell my hon. friend how this is made up. There is $20,000,000 of the Grand Trunk Pacific Railway Company secured by second mortgages on the western division, guaranteed by the Grand Trunk Railway Company of Canada, and $25,000,000 representing two loans made, one in 1909 and the other in 1913 by the Dominion of Canada, guaranteed by the Grand Trunk Railway Company of Canada. That makes $45,000,000. In addition to that there is $48,000,000, representing debenture stock of the Grand Trunk Pacific Railway Company guaranteed by the Grand Trunk Railway Company of Canada. In addition to that, there is some further liability which makes a total of about $97,000,000. That $97,000,000 means an interest liability of about $4,000,000 per annum on the part of the Grand Trunk Railway Company of Canada in respect of its guarantee. There is some overlapping, and in order that the House may not be confused by the overlapping, I should say that the total securities outstanding of the Grand Trunk Pacific Railway Company guaranteed by both the Dominion Government and the Grand Trunk Railway Company of Canada, aggregate something over $200,000,000.
I think I mentioned the fact that there were guarantees on the branch lines by the provinces of Alberta and Saskatchewan. That brings us down to the present year. We had the Drayton-Acworth report, recommending that in order to meet the difficulties of the railway situation, the Government of Canada should take over the Canadian Northern, as we did, and should also take over the Grand Trunk Pacific Railway Company and the Grand Trunk Railway Company of Canada.
Early in 1918, there were some negotiations with respect to the matter, but they came to nothing. Last year when the Prime Minister and certain of his colleagues were overseas, the question was taken up with the Grand Trunk Railway Company which, I may say, desired some assistance from the Government about July of last year. It transpired afterwards that they were able to arrange otherwise; but the matter was taken up with Mr. Smithers and the Board of Directors of the Grand Trunk Railway Company, by the Prime Minister and his colleagues overseas.
I desire to inform the House as to the offer which was then made by the Government of Canada and as to the counter-offer which was made by the Grand Trunk Rail-

way Company of Canada. The House will then understand the situation practically down to the present time. As I said to the leader of the Opposition (Mr. McKenzie) if, when I have concluded my remarks in the course of this discussion upon the resolution, there is further information that he requires and I can get it, it, of course, goes without saying that I shall be only too glad to give it to the House. I do not know what correspondence there was in the time of the Government which held power up to 1911, and personally I cannot see that it has much bearing on the question before us to-day, because agreements were entered into which were validated by legislation. It, therefore, appears to me that the legislation discloses the situation, and the correspondence would not be helpful. If, however, my hon. friend has in mind any particular correspondence, I shall be glad to endeavour to get it. This is the offer made on behalf of the Government of Canada last July by the Minister of the Interior (Mr. Meighen). It is a little long, but I hope the House will have patience:
Dear Mr. Smithers:

Some time ago the Government of Canada was informed on behalf of the Board of Directors of the Grand Trunk Railway Company that this company would not be able, without Government assistance, to meet certain maturities falling due on the 1st and 15th of the present month.
It was thought of advantage that representatives of the Government should, on the occasion of their visit to England, to attend the Imperial War Conference, take the opportunity of conferring with yourself and your directorate on the general subject of Grand Trunk obligations and finance. Accordingly, the Hon. Mr. Calder and myself have had four conferences with you, at two of which you were accompanied by certain associates on the Board.
At the last conference you suggested that I should lay before you in writing the position taken by the Government and, in as definite a form as possible, its concrete proposals.
It may be assumed that the difficulties in which the company now finds itself arise from two main causes:-
(1)	The obligations into which the company entered in 1903 and 1904 with respect to the Grand Trunk Pacific Railway Company;
(2)	War conditions as to operation and finance.
As to the latter cause it is not unfair to say that its incidence has fallen chiefly, if not wholly, in the years 1917 and 1918. On the contrary, the difficulties of the Grand Trunk Railway Company, which are the direct outcome of its Grand Trunk Pacific obligations, are of much longer date. This latter company is in every sense subsidiary to, and its stock is wholly owned by the Grand Trunk Company. To this subsidiary company the Government of Canada came, by way of assistance, as far back as 1909, with a loan of $10,000,000. Another loan of $15,000,000 was made in 1913. A further loan of $6,000,000 was made in 1914 on a pledge of bonds. Its securities were further

guaranteed by legislation of that year to the extent of $16,000,000. In 1916 a loan of $8,000,000 was made. In 1917, a loan of $7,500,000 was authorized and advanced, and in the spring of this year a further loan of $7,500,000 was authorized by Parliament. Mean-tirne, the ever-increasing interest obligation binding on the Grand Trunk Railway Company towards its subsidiary company were not paid by the Grand Trunk Railway Company, but were taken care of out of the proceeds of loans thus made by the Government of Canada. These obligations at the present time amount to very considerably over $5,000,000 per annum and in January 1923 increase to over $7,000,000 per annum.
Those are the figures given in the Dray-ton-Acworth report.
In the same conjunction it must also be remembered that the Grand Trunk Pacific Company has not assumed or attempted to discharge its rental obligations to the Government of Canada with respect to the National Transcontinental Railway, which obligations while not formally assumed by the Government, have in practice been shouldered by the Dominion. This extra burden is a matter of very considerable magnitude.
I refer to the outstanding facts related in the preceding paragraph for the purpose of indicating what has through recent years been the attitude of the Canadian Government and people toward Grand Trunk enterprises.
It is at this point that the Canadian Government is invited to enter upon a still wider field of assistance by assuming the liabilities in respect of Grand Trunk securities themselves.
We had been asked to render some assistance in July.
Through the course of the' various steps recalled above, public opinion in our country has become more and more opposed to a continuance of the practice of assisting financially railways that were in private hands. Consequently, at the opening of our negotiations we stated to you that we did not believe that continued further assistance under present conditions could be justified.
In order, however, that there might be reasonable opportunity for negotiations, we recommended to the Minister of Finance that funds be provided to enable the company to meet maturities falling due in July. This has been and is being arranged.
I may say that it was not necessary to go on with it.
Throughout the negotiations and indeed prior thereto, it has been made clear to your Company that the obligations of the Grand Trunk Company to the Grand Trunk Pacific Company could not be ignored and that the Government could not undertake to assume the indebtedness of and to operate the Grand Trunk Pacific and branch lines thereof, and to relieve the Grand Trunk of responsibility therefor, while the Grand Trunk Railway itself, as a subsidiary of which and indeed as an extension of which the Grand Trunk Pacific was built, remained In independent bands. Accordingly, in the month of February last, after careful consideration and in pursuance of the recommendation of what is commonly known as the Drayton-Acworth Report, there were made to your Company the following proposals:

(1) The Government to take over the Grand Trunk Pacific Railway and branch lines and the Grand Trunk Railway Company; to acquire all assets, and to assume all obligations of both Companies.
(2 ) The Government to make annual payment of $2,500,000 for the first three years, $3,000,000 for the succeeding five years, and $3,600,000 annually thereafter; such sums to be distributed by the Grand Trunk management, as they might determine, among holders of 4 per cent Guaranteed and other stocks.
It was intended that the taking over should be by rental over a long period of years, as might be agreed, with a provision for purchase.
Should such terms not be accepted, it was suggested that the amounts in question might be submitted to arbitration. These proposals met with no acceptance.
Our present conference, extending over the past months have resulted in little progress- the only practical step being indeed the assistance referred to above as advanced by the Government. As intimated above, such assistance cannot under present conditions be continued.
We are now prepared to abide by the proposals submitted to you in February last as to acquisition or we are prepared on behalf of the Government to submit the entire question of remuneration to a Board of Arbitration on the following general terms :

(1)	The Board to consist of three persons; one to be appointed by the Grand Trunk Company, one by the Government of Canada, and the two so appointed to select a third, or, if they fail to agree, the third to be selected by a majority of the following: the Judge of the Exchequer Court of Canada, the Chief Justice of the Supreme Court of Canada, the Chief Justice of the Province of Ontario.
(2)	The Board to have full power as to the procuring and acceptance of evidence
(3)	The award to be by way of annual rental for a term of 999 years; the Board to have power to vary the rental for two or more periods of years. The Government to have the option of purchase on the basis of and during the term of the final rental at the end of any year and on one-year's notice at twenty-five times the annual final rental.
(4)	Conditions arising or that have arisen out of the war not to be taken into account in determining the rental value.
Should the Company desire, the Guaranteed Stock may be treated as an obligation in the same way as the Company's Bonds.
I would be glad to be advised whether the above specific proposal is acceptable or if not, whether the general terms of arbitration outlined above are satisfactory. Should either alternative be favourably received we may then enter upon discussion and negotiation as to further necessary details.
Tours very truly,
(Sgd.) Arthur Meighen. Alfred W. Smithers, Esq.,
Chairman of the Board of Directors,
Grand Trunk Railway Company,
9 New Broad Street,

That was the offer of the Government of Canada-an offer along the lines suggested in the Drayton-Acworth report. But in addition to that, in case that offer was not
acceptable to the Grand Trunk Railway Company, the Government of Canada offered to leave to arbitration the question of the rental to be paid. I have seen some reports emanating from London to the effect that the Government was not dealing as fairly with the Grand Trunk as with the Canadian Northern. Well, the Government had the question of wh'at it should pay for the stock of the Canadian Northern determined by arbitration, a maximum being fixed as a safeguard against an unduly high award. But here we are not setting any maximum amount; we offered to arbitrate as to the price we should pay.

About $8,000,000.

-or you were prepared to leave the whole question of the amount to he paid to arbitration. At our meeting yesterday I proposed that the Government should pay a net annual sum of 977,000 pounds-

-being the amount of net earnings for the year 1913, the last normal year before the war, and thus following the course pursued by the British Government towards the British Railways, and leave to arbitration what further sum if any, the shareholders are entitled to in respect of the prospective value of the undertaking that must arise from the development of the Dominion. Was the offer made by the Government intended to relieve the Grand Trunk of their obligations in respect of the Grand Trunk Pacific?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
It was so stated. The Government said: "We realize the Grand Trunk Railway Company cannot meet its obligations in respect of the Grand Trunk Pacific." Everybody realizes that. The Drayton-Acworth report says so; it says: "Deal generously with them." We say so too. The Government said: "We will assume all the liabilities of the Grand Trunk Pacific Railway Company (and, remember, we have been carrying them), assume all the liabilities of the Grand Trunk Railway Company, take a lease for 999 years and pay you the amount mentioned in Mr. fSIr Thomas White.]
Meighen's letter by way of rental; or, if you are not satisfied with that, we will arbitrate."
The Grand Trunk said, " No, we will not do that, but we make you a counter offer in which we ignore altogether our liabilities in respect of the Grand Trunk Pacific; we want the Government to take care of that, and, in addition, to pay us on the basis of what we regard as the value of Grand Trunk shares, without the slightest regard to our liability towards the Grand Trunk Pacific Railway." Now, the negotiations ended. I read to the House the other day the correspondence which had taken place with the Grand Trunk Pacific Company with respect to two matters: First, default which was apprehended on March 1, and second, the discontinuance of the operation of the Grand Trunk Railway system.
That is default in payment of interest?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: It was apprehended. Now, let me say with regard to the last vote of $7,500,000 made last year by Parliament, that the Government, after Sir Robert Borden and his colleagues had returned, and after we were aware that an impasse had been reached, felt they must continue to pay that $7,500,000 to the Grand Trunk Pacific Railway Company, because it had been voted by Parliament. It would have been legal on the part of the Government to have discontinued payment under that vote last fall, because all votes made by Parliament are really subject to the Government paying them out. But when Parliament votes a certain sum the view that governments take-at least, the view that I have always understood they should take-is that Parliament intended that the money voted should be devoted to the purposes for which the vote was made. Therefore, the Government has paid out to the Grand Trunk Pacific Railway Company the $7,500,000 which was voted last year, tthe proceeds of which have not been entirely used.
May I ask if you deduct from the $7,500,000 the interest charges for which the Grand Trunk was liable for the Grand Trunk Pacific?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
No, the $7,500,-
000 paid the fixed charges on the Grand Trunk Pacific Railway Company; that is to say, the interest upon the securities guaranteed by the Dominion Government and guaranteed by the Grand Trunk Railway Company of Canada, and also the deficit up to the time the vote was exhausted. The $7,500,000 was not sufficient for the

past year. In February the vote was exhausted and the Grand Trunk Pacific Railway Company notified the Government that they apprehended they would have to make default on March 1 in respect to interest upon securities maturing due in London, and called the attention of the Government to the serious situation which would arise if funds were not provided for that purpose. The reply which I made to them is contained in a letter which is on Hansard. We stated that the last of the money, about $1,000,000, had been paid over to meet deficit on operating expenses in accordance with the certificate of the Grand Trunk Railway officials themselves, approved by the Deputy Minister of Railways, and that no question could arise as to that money being properly applied to meet deficit on operation before application was made of any part of it to meet interest upon securities; and I said further that it would be for the directors of the Grand Trunk Railway Company to consider what were their , responsibilities towards that interest which was falling due in London upon securities of the Grand Trunk Pacific Railway Company which they had guaranteed. Now, the Government was prepared for default, if it had occurred, because we had made up our minds that as long as negotiations with the Grand Trunk Railway Company of Canada -to use the language which I employed- " remained in their present unsatisfactory condition," the Dominion Government would not ask Parliament to vote any further sums.
Hear, hear.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: We had taken that view, not hastily. The matter had been under deliberation for weeks and months and the Government had come to the conclusion, and had notified that conclusion to the responsible officers of the Grand Trunk Pacific Railway Company, and of the Grand Trunk Railway Company of Canada, that when that money became exhausted the Dominion Government would not bring down a further vote, as had been done during the last three years, by way of loans to the Grand Trunk Pacific Railway Company for the purpose of meeting fixed charges and deficit on operating expenses.

The inference from the letter of Mr. Smithers, in January, 1918, is that the Government at that time, in January, 1918, had opened negotiations with the Grand Trunk Railway to purchase the Grand Trunk Railway and all their system. Was that the unanimous policy of the Government in January, 1918, to purchase all those roads?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Having regard to the Grand Trunk Pacific situation and the liability which it involved, and the fact also that we had been asked for assistance by the Grand Trunk Railway Company, in July negotiations were taken up. But at an earlier date, in January, 1918, the Prime Minister had made an offer to the Grand Trunk Railway Company practically in pursuance of the Drayton-Acwotth report.
Negotiations were opened by the Government?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Yes. The Grand Trunk Pacific Railway Company and the Grand Trunk Railway Company were coming every year to the Government and saying, "Vote us $7,500,000 or $8,000,000 to keep the Grand Trunk Pacific going, but don't call upon the Grand Trunk Railway Company for anything." Now, that could not go on, and the Government therefore opened negotiations with a view to clearing up the entire situation. The Government had been bearing all the responsibility of the Grand Trunk Pacific, and the Grand Trunk Railway Company of Canada expected it to continue bearing all the responsibility. The situation had to be cleaned up. The hon. Minister of the Interior (Mr. Meighen) says he thinks there was a communication from the Grand Trunk Railway Company prior to our offer. I shall inquire as to that; but at all events, I do not know that it is indispensable to the discussion of the matter because the situation speaks for itself.
Before you get away from the responsibility of the Grand Trunk, may I ask, how did they get relieved of responsibility with regard to the Transcontinental?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
I am coming to that. I will summarize later. That interest was paid on March 1st, I believe-I did not hear anything to the contrary, and I should have heard if it had not been paid. Now, that difficulty was overcome, and the next thing that happened was, without any previous intimation or discussion at all, a notice-which I described in a cable to Mr. Smithers as peremptory-a notice on Thursday,! think, that on the following Monday, by reason of the fact that the freight rates in the West were not high enough to enable _the Grand Trunk Pacific to operate without "a loss, they would have to close that system. Without any discussion, without any previous intimation, the ultimatum was served

upon the Government. " We are going to close down the Grand Trunk Pacific Railway system unless-" it was not so stated, but the inference is irresistible- "-unless the Government does what the Government said it would not do, namely, give us a further vote to enable us to carry on." Now, it is a pretty serious thing to close down a transcontinental railway system of 2,700 miles of main line and branches. The notification was in explicit terms: " We cannot go on." They knew that the Government had taken the view that it would not recommend to Parliament to vote any further money. What was the Government to do? I am frank to say that I do not believe the Grand Trunk Railway Company officials, or the Grand Trunk Pacific Railway officials believed that the Government had power to deal with the situation.
Hear, hear.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
I do not like to impute motives, but it is my opinion that they did not realize that the Government had power to deal with the question, notwithstanding that Parliament was in session. Why do I say that? In adverting to that, I reply to the remarks of my hon. friend the leader of the Opposition about the courts affording an adequate remedy. We did not overlook the courts, but the courts afford no adequate remedy to the cessation of operations on a system such as the Grand Trunk Pacific railway. If my hon. friend, who is a good lawyer and who has been a judge, will take the trouble to look at the legislation upon the subject, and upon the jurisdiction of the Exchequer Court, he will find that what I have stated is absolutely correct. He will find further, that even as to the jurisdiction, if it does not exist in the Exchequer Court as to the appointment of a receiver, it must be on an application for foreclosure and sale. Before application can be made for foreclosure and sale of a railway company, default must exist, and a certain time elapse under the provisions of whatever mortgage or other instrument has been taken as security. The Dominion Government was not in a position to make application to the Exchequer Court for a receiver, because it could not prove default. The position was then that the Government could not resort to the Exchequer Court. The Exchequer Court would have no jurisdiction to make an order.
We had to consider what we would do to prevent a great railway system from closing down with inconvenience not only to the people of the West but to the people of Canada generally. We did not hesitate 
to make a clean-cut case of it, and the Dominion Government fell back upon the War Measures Act, which gives jurisdiction in the matter of railways, and appointed my hon. friend the Minister of Railways and Canals (Mr. Reid) a receiver.
Why did we appoint him a receiver? To ensure the continued operation of a system so essential to the convenience and welfare of the great communities which it serves. Let me say further to the leader of the Opposition that the Exchequer Court has no jurisdiction to appoint a receiver of a telegraph company. Embraced in a system such as the Grand Trunk Pacific there is not only the railway system itself but the telegraph system, the development company with the assets I mentioned previously, the steamship company, and all those other auxiliary or subsidiary enterprises.
There is a great lack in the railway legislation of Canada which some day will have to be remedied by this House in regard to the jurisdiction of the court to deal with a system as compared with an individual [DOT] railway. Some day that will have to receive attention.
Now, the Government appointed a receiver. Lest it should be thought that further negotiations would have resulted in bringing about an understanding

How does the minister understand this section 6 of the Winding-up Act, which says:
"This Act applies to all corporations incorporated under the authority of an Act of the Parliament of Canada."
I would suppose that would be sufficiently comprehensive to include a telegraph company, or any company incorporated by this Parliament, or under the authority of this Parliament, and that this company would come within a section of that kind.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
I am informed on the highest legal authority that there is no jurisdiction in the Exchequer Court to deal with the question of a receivership for the system. There is this further consideration : Supposing that in several of the provinces of Canada applications were made to the courts for the appointment of not a receiver, but many receivers, for a railway system of this character and for all its subsidiaries, what a situation you would have! tit would paralyse the operation of the system. There is not to-day any existing legislation providing for any effectual remedy through a receivership for a railway system such as the Grand Trunk Pacific and its subsidiaries.

In order that there may not be any doubt in the minds of any of the members of the committee that the Grand Trunk intended that notice to mean that they would close down by reason of lack of funds, I may state that I received a further cable from Mr. Smithers, in which he stated-I am afraid I cannot lay my hands on it just at the moment-that the fact that they had no funds made it necessary that they should notify the Government as they did. There is no question about it; the issue is clear-cut-the Dominion Government to furnish the money or the Grand Trunk to cease operations.
That brings us down to the present time and to this resolution that is before the House. Although the Government has plenary jurisdiction under the	War
Measures Act, action having been taken when Parliament is in session, it is of course proper that Parliament should deal with this Order in Council, validate it, approve it, and translate it into an Act of Parliament, in order that no question can arise whatever with regard to its validity.
Let me summarize the National Transcontinental railway situation including the Grand Trunk Pacific railway which is embraced in it:
An agreement made in 1903 to build a line from Moncton to the tide-waters of the Pacific-a great enterprise.
The Government of Canada to build the line from Moncton to Winnipeg, which cost in the neighbourhood of $170,000,000 without interest.
The Grand Trunk Pacific Railway Company to construct the lines and its subsidiaries from Winnipeg to Prince Rupert.
The Grand Trunk Railway Company to lease the eastern division of the National Transcontinental railway for a period of 50 years after seven of which they were to pay an annual rental and also any deficit on operating account. That was to be 3 per cent upon the cost which would amount to about $5,000,000 or 3 per cent on $170,000,000. Let us say $4,000,000 to be conservative, because it may be said that I have overstated the amount. I do not think I have but I do not desire to raise any controversy as to that.
The Grand Trunk Railway Company would be the proprietor of the entire system by holding all the stock in the Grand Trunk Pacific Railway Company.
What happens? The Grand Trunk Pacific, and the Grand Trunk Railway Company, as a party in the matter, say: We cannot lease the National Transcontinental railway. They put it on various grounds
but the ground is perfectly obvious; they could not lease the National Transcontinental railway and pay the rental of $4,000,000 or $5,000,000. They simply could not do it. The Dominion Government gives its guarantees, the Grand Trunk gives its guarantees, the western division is built at a cost of something all together, if you include deficits and fixed charges for the past three years, over $200,000,000. The Dominion Government is interested in this to the extent of $100,000,000 and the Grand Trunk's interest almost a like sum. The Grand Trunk Pacific had said to the Dominion Government: We cannot lease the eastern division of the National Transcontinental railway. The Grand Trunk Railway Company say to the Dominion: We want to assume no responsibility for the Grand Trunk Pacific; take the whole thing off our hands from Moncton to Prince Rupert That is the statement. Now I do not believe that this is a position which the Grand Trunk Railway Company can hold.
It should not be allowed to.	.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I do not believe that is a position the Grand Trunk Railway Company should hold. The Government and the people of this country are very friendly to the Grand Trunk Railway Company, as they are to all British enterprises in this country so far as I know. But the people of Canada, I believe, will not support the Government in continuing the generous policy which it has pursued during the last three years of loaning seven and a half or eight million dollars yearly to pay off the liabilities in respect of the Grand Trunk Pacific, including the interest upon the securities guaranteed by_ the Grand Trunk Railway Company-I do not believe it. That is the position to-day. The Government is in possession as receiver. The resolution indicates the powers and duties of the receiver, and enlarges the jurisdiction of the Exchequer Court to deal with whatever situations may arise. It is not the intention of the Government to bring down a further vote while, as I stated in my communication to the Grand Trunk Railway Company, the negotiations between that company and the Dominion remain in their present unsatisfactory condition. It seems to me that the next move is on the part of the Grand Trunk Railway Company.

Before the hon. gentleman closes his very clear and excellent speech, would he be good enough to tell

the committee what the Government proposes to do? The Government has taken the Grand Trunk Pacific Railway-the hon. gentleman has dealt with that fully in his speech-but what does the Government propose to do now that it has the line in its hands, or what is it thinking of doing?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: What we are doing now is passing this resolution, but my hon. friend wishes to know what will be the policy of the Government?
Yes.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: The policy of the Government, speaking frankly to my hon. friend, will be what it has been in the past. There have been negotiations between the Grand Trunk Railway Company of Canada and the Dominion, and in our view the attitude of the Board of Directors of the Grand Trunk Company has not been a reasonable one, because they have steadfastly refused to recognize the liabilities in respect of the Grand Trunk Pacific Railway; and I say that negotiations with the Grand Trunk Company are not possible until that company's liabilities in respect of the Grand Trunk Pacific Railway are regarded as a factor, an important factor, in those negotiations. I do not go the distance of saying-I have never gone so far as to say so-that this matter Should be looked upon in a hard and fast business way; that is to say that we should set off against any net earnings of the Grand Trunk Railway Company of Canada, actual or prospective so far as we can estimate, the full amount of the deficit for fixed charges and operating expenses of the Grand Trunk Pacific, because if we did, it would wipe out absolutely all equity in Grand Trunk Railway shares. We have never taken that view.

The minister did not
answer my question. What I meant is what is the Government going to do now that it has the Grand Trunk Pacific Railway in its hands?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: We are going to carry on.

What are you going
to do?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I repeat that we are going to carry on.
Are you going to own the railway?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
We are carrying on as receiver at the present time. We are maintaining the service upon which great 
communities of this country depend from day to day. That is the immediate reason for the appointment of a receiver. What we shall do later on will be as we may determine, but I may say to my hon. friend that unless a satisfactory situation ensues the Dominion Government will be obliged to have recourse to whatever legal remedies it may have, and it has many.

And it may be
a receivership for the Grand Trunk?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I pass no opinion as to that. I have endeavoured to expound to the House as clearly as I could, and I am afraid at too great length, the situation, because this is an important transaction. Do not let me give the House or the country the impression that the Government desires to deal harshly with, or to exact the pound of flesh from, the Grand Trunk Railway Company of Canada; we have not done so, and we do not intend to do so; but we do not intend to negotiate upon a basis in which all the prospective earnings are to be capitalized, for the Grand Trunk, and all the liabilities of that company, in respect to the Grand Trunk Pacific, are to be ignored. As I said the next move is from the Grand Trunk Railway Company of Canada.

The hon. gentleman has
stated that the next move should be on the part of the Grand Trunk. It seems to me that the Government should hold the Grand Trunk Company liable for the obligations which it has not met in the past, and therefore the next move should be on the part of the Government, in order to hold the company to its obligations which the hon. gentleman states it has absolutely ignored.
The action taken by the Government so far, does not seem to be very consistent, lit passed an Order in Council and took possession of the railway before it had actually made default.

Done deliberately.
Mr. GA'HILL:	The receiver stated that
he had taken possession on the morning of Monday, March 10, at one o'clock, and the company had notified the 'Government that it might default on and after the. 10th of March.	*

The hon. gentleman is
wrong. The company notified the Government that it would default on or before the 10th of March.
Mr. CAiHOjLL:	Was it not on or after
the 10th?
No, on or before the 10th.

But the Government did
not give the company any opportunity of ceasing on the 10th. It took possession before, and this makes it appear to the overseas investors that the Government is adopting summary action and trying to force the company's hand. It looks very much like a horse trading operation, where one side is trying to take advantage of the other.
No.

It looks very much like
it. The Acting Prime Minister referred quite frequently to the Drayton-Aeworth Report and advised all hon. members to read it, and I think it is very good advice. I think that Report should be read by all of us; there are very many passages in it that are well worthy of careful perusal. The Acting Prime Minister said the commissioners recommended that the Government should take this road over, but he omitted to read one further paragraph. I will supply the omission:
1.	That the Government do not acquire or undertake to operate any further railways; but
2.	That these three railways, Canadian Northern, Grand Trunk, and Grand Trunk Pacific, be transferred by Act of Parliament to an independent Board of Trustees (incorporated as a company), constituted as we shall hereafter describe.
These recommendations, from our point of view, hang together and must be regarded as inseparable. We do not recommend the transfer of the three companies at all, unless our recommendations as to the method to be followed are also substantially accepted. That the Government should Itself take over the railways, and they should then be operated under the control of a Parliamentary Minister of Railways, is a policy which in our judgment would not be in the best interest of Canada.
The commissioners pointed out in various places through the report that they would not under any consideration recommend the Government taking over the road and operating it. I think the Prime Minister is somewhat in error in saying that the Government railways are being operated as recommended by the Drayton-Aeworth report, because they are actually being operated by a board of about fifteen directors, whereas the recommendation of the Drayton-Aeworth report was that the directorate should consist of five members. The operation is carried on as a political proposition. The directors are appointed by the Minister of Railways, and I think I am safe in saying that one qualification all possess is that they supported the Union Government at the last election. There i3 not a known railway man in the whole aggregation of directors, outside of Mr. Hanna, Mackenzie and Mann's appointee, who was associated with Mackenzie and Mann in practically all their undertakings in this country during the last twenty years. Mr. C.	M. Hamilton, of McTaggart, another of the directors, is a farmer, and I believe, a very good man; but I understand also that he made way for his Conservative opponent in the last election and was a supporter of the Union Government. Apparently this is his reward. Mr. Thomas Cantley, of New Glasgow, and Mr. Barnhill, of St-. John, N.B., are presidents of steel companies. Sir H. Laporte, of Montreal, who is on practically all the Government commissions, is a wholesale grocer. Mr. Jones, of Montreal, is in the cement and steel business. Then there are Mr. Bell, of Ottawa, Mr. Riley, of Winnipeg, a broker; Mr. Hobson, of Hamilton, president of a steel company there. The others were the former directors of the Canadian Northern.
The grabbing, as it were, of these railways does not solve the railway problem of Canada. The great difficulty is that we have not sufficient traffic to make the railroads pay, and the reason why we have not sufficient traffic is that we have not sufficient population.
Why did we build them?
That is a question I would like the Government to answer.
Oh, oh.

The Drayton-Aeworth report says:
We may put the same thing in another way. The growth of the mileage has far outstripped the growth of the population. In 1901, with a population of 5,371,315, Canada had 18,140 miles of railway in operation; roughly, a mile of railway for every 300 inhabitants. In 1911, the population had increased 34 per cent to 7,206,643, while the mileage had increased by 40 per cent to 25,400 miles; a mile of railway to every 284 inhabitants.
Mark you, in 1911 we had a mile of railway to every 284 people. There was an election in that year. The report goes on to say:
Since 1911, the population has, it is understood, not much increased, but the railway mileage open and under construction has grown to 40,584 miles. In other words, Canada has today, taking the present population as 7,500,000, only 185 inhabitants to support each mile of railway. Taking the four western provinces by themselves, there are only two-thirds of this number for each mile of railway.
That refers to the period between 1911 and 1916, in respect of which hon. gentle-

men will not attempt to put the responsibility for railway conditions upon members on this side. It may be said that before 1911 a railway policy had been inaugurated, and so on. That is quite true as applied to the period from 1896; but at the same time a policy of immigration and colonization was carried out by the Government which went out of power in 1911. That policy, which caused the country to be settled as railways were built, continued from 1896 to 1911. The railways did not get ahead of the population, nor was the population much behind the railways; the ratio -was properly preserved. But between 1911 and 1917, hon. gentlemen opposite seemed to forget all about the immigration and colonization policy, and they constructed railroads all over the country. The friends of railway operators and contractors were in power at that time.
It does not make much difference whether you hand this money over to the Grand Trunk Pacific and let them pay it out to cover operating deficits, or pay it out yourself. The difficulty is that you may pay a great deal more to operate the road as a Government undertaking. The question for us to solve is: How are we to handle those railroads? The first consideration should be: What management do you propose? How do you hope to manage these roads? The Lrayton-Acworth report goes very fully into that; in no sense does it recommend that the roads be taken over by Canada if they are to be operated by the Government. The report recommends that they be operated by a commission, and points out how the commission should be formed. I do not say that I agree with everything in the Drayton-Acworth report, but apparently the only things in that report that the Government agree with are the things that suit them and their friends. There is no mention in the report of paying the Canadian Northern people $10,800,000 for a portion of their stock; on the contrary, that stock was condemned as of no value. We have the farce of an arbitration proceeding in Toronto which decides that we shall pay out this $10,800,000; yet we have not acquired all the stock; we do not know who are the owmers of ten per cent of that stock. It is understood, however, mat this stock is owned by some of the friends of the Mackenzie and Mann interests.
Last year the Prime Minister announced that negotiations were to be started for the taking over of the Grand Trunk Pacific. Various members of the Government carpet-bagged back and forth across the ocean 
last year; our esteemed friend Clifford Sif-ton also was on these tours. If that speaking tube that he uses so well could tell a tale, it could inform us very much better about this railway situation than we have been informed this afternoon.
The chief trouble in connection with our railway situation is the land question. The Canadian Northern runs through millions of acres of vacant lands held by speculators throughout Western Canada and by competing railway companies. If our railroads run through vacant lands and produce no traffic, necessarily we must lose money on the operation. Until this land question is satisfactorily settled, the roads which run through these unoccupied areas cannot possibly make money. Even the tariff enters into railroad operation. If you sweep the tariff wall away in Western Canada and inaugurate a sane land policy, causing the land held by speculators in the West to be put into use and to create traffic for the roads which we own, we would have very little trouble with the railway situation. If you have people on the lines of the railways, the railways will take care of themselves. We have one prosperous railway system; the Canadian Pacific is making money. In fact, we are forcing money on them that they do not require. They are earning so much that we expect to get part of it back, because they are, earning more than the country is supposed to allow them. But that line runs through territory that is developed. We have not too much railway mileage; we have too little population, and no policy which would have the effect of increasing it.
If the Minister of Immigration and Colonization (Mr. Calder) would spend more time in looking after the colonization of the country and less in convincing himself that he is a Liberal, it would be much better for the railways of this country. On the Transcontinental east of here, from Cochrane east, all through the province of Quebec, there is the poorest kind of service, a service that is heart-breaking to settlers going into that country. The pioneers going_into that country cannot get cars to handle their wood. Here is an undertaking that cost from $50,000 to $60,000 a mile to build, and sufficient rolling stock is not provided. The road is well built; the country is fairly well settled; but how can the road ever hope to pay if you do not handle the .traffic on it and do not encourage the traffic there. If the Minister of Immigration and Colonization would take a trip through that country if he would look after the traffic of that country and see that the railroad gave pro-

per facilities for handling the wood and other products of that country, instead of losing thousands of people from Quebec and Northern Ontario. If that were done, that road, instead of losing a great deal of money would, in a few years, prove a profitable enterprise. But if you start out with the avowed intention of killing the settlement, of course, the road cannot pay. That is bound to be the result if you will not give a proper service, and people are, therefore, afraid to go in. I know of instances on the Transcontinental last year where people drew out wood, having been promised that they would get cars. The wood was worth $5 a cord. They took out the wood, but they could not sell it, because there were no cars to take the wood away. In the spring of the year, the brokers and lawyers oaime along and bought that wood at from $2.50 to $3 a cord, and a few weeks afterwards they were able to secure cars. Such occurrences will kill settlement in any country. There has been no attempt to give service on the Transcontinental since it has been built, and unless you give service-
The Grand Trunk undertook to do that.

The Grand Trunk undertook to do that, and the Dominion Government, of which my hon. friends are members, relieved the Grand Trunk of their responsibility, and when they relieved them of that responsibility, I think the Grand Trunk was quite justified in believing that they would also be relieved of the Grand Trunk Pacific responsibility.
Mr. NICKLE. Why?

The Transcontinental is
the connecting link between the old Grand Trunk and the Grand Trunk Pacific. The Grand Trunk are now in the position of owning a railroad in the west with no connecting link from Winnipeg to the East. That connecting link was taken from them by the Government of this country, and when that wias done, I think the Grand 'Trunk were quite right in assuming that the Government were also going to relieve them of the Grand Trunk Pacific.

Does the hon. member
think that the Grand Trunk should be relieved of its liability or not?

I am not debating the
point whether it should be relieved of its liability or not. If it should not be relieved, the Government should have taken action when they relieved that company of the Transcontinental. They relieved the Grand
Trunk of the connecting link. It is a debatable question whether they should be relieved or not. The Grand Trunk Railway Company of Canada have not received from the Dominion of Canada $10,000,000 altogether for the construction of railroads in Canada. The Grand Trunk was a pioneer road during its whole career. It is owned by British people in the old country who invested their money here for the development of Canada. The Canadian Pacific came along and got in the neighbourhood of $100,000,000 from the Treasury of Canada. The Grand Trunk got a few million dollars to build a conecting link from the boundary line down to Portland.

The report here will show that they did not get anything which they
did not pay back except a few million to build a road from Portland to the boundary
They had assistance from the municipalities through which they went, and they did not pay anything back.

I am not speaking about the municipalities; I am speaking about the Government. My own county of Pontiac has assisted roads by bonuses, and I do not think that is quite the right thing to do. I think it is a mistake. But we are not speaking about the assistance they got from the various municipalities; we are speaking about the assistance they got from the Government. As they have not received nearly as much assistance from this country as the Canadian Pacific or the Canadian Northern has, I think they are justified in asking for fair treatment in this matter. I think they are justified in asking that they be released from the Grand Trunk Pacific obligation, especially as they have been released from the Transcontinental obligation, as that leaves them without any-connecting link whatever. We are rushing into this thing haphazard with apparently no policy. The Government say that they are being guided by the Drayton-Acworth Report, but, apart from the matter of taking over the road, they are not following the report in regard to management or operation or payment for the road. They are simply taking the road and throwing it into the hands of the Canadian Northern crowd, the Mackenzie and Mann outfit, who apparently want to grab the Grand Trunk and the Grand Trunk Pacific. If there is an obligation on the part of the Grand Trunk, that obligation should easily be determined between the railway company

and the Government. It is only in connection with the Grand Trunk guarantees, and has nothing to do with the Grand Trunk Railway Company itself, because the Gr nd Trunk Railway Company claim that they are able to operate. They have never made default in their operations or in paying interest on their bonds. The only operation they are being " crowded " on is their guarantees of the Grand Trunk Pacific bonds. It seems that the Government think the Grand Trunk should be [DOT] relieved of that-and the Acting Prime Minister (Sir Thomas White) apparently thinks so himself, because he says the Government offered them a certain amount of money which would relieve them of the obligation. He says: If they insist on taking up the Grand Trunk Pacific obligation, they have no equity whatsoever. Yet he says that they should be relieved of the responsibilities of the Grand Trunk Pacific.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: No.

Well, it is practically that, is it not? The Acting Prime Minister says that the Grand Trunk, if they are held responsible regarding their obligations to the Grand Trunk Pacific, have no equity. Yet he says that the Government is willing to pay them an equity in the road. And he also says, if I understood him correctly, they would claim the relieving of the liability so far as the Grand Trunk Railway Company was concerned.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: My hon. friend misquotes me. I did state that if the liability of the Grand Trunk in respect to the Grand Trunk Pacific were taken fully into account, the value of the Grand Trunk shares would be practically nil; and I said, and said it with emphasis, that in our negotiations with the Grand Trunk Railway Company, their liabilities in respect of the Grand Trunk Pacific must be regarded as an important factor bearing upon the question of what we shall in our generosity allow them.

If the Acting Prime Minister admits the principle that the Grand Trunk have no equity in the 'Grand Trunk Pacific, then why does he offer them this money at all? It seems an unreasonable proposition that he should offer them some $3,000,000 a year for something in which they have no equity, unless he admits the principle that he should relieve them of the Grand Trunk Pacific liability; and if he admits that principle, then I think they can justly state whether they want to sell the Grand Trunk 
Railway to the Government or not. I think they would be justified in saying: We will put a price on it, or we will not, just as they see fit, so long as they are not in default. The Grand Trunk themselves are probably anxious and quite willing to get rid of the Grand Trunk Pacific, and I think that, by this action taken by the Government, they have done so, because the Government have jumped in summarily and taken possession, without the Grand Trunk making default. I think before the Government gets through they will find they have relieved the Grand Trunk of the Grand Trunk Pacific, and they will have no further hold on the Grand Trunk.
With regard to the earnings, the minister says that it will take from $7,000,000 to $8,000,000 a year to pay the deficits. I have here a statement of the Canadian Northern gross earnings. For September, 1918, the gross earnings were $4,050,700, as compared with $3,341,500 for the same period in the previous year-an increase of $709,200. Operating expenses were $4,109,000 compared with $2,915,800 for the year previous, so that net earnings of $425,900 for September, 1917 have been turned into a deficit of $58,100 for the same month of 1918. The operating expenses work out on a similar basis. So I think it might have been better to wait a while and leave the operation of the Grand Trunk Pacific to the Grand Trunk until some amicable arrangement had been arrived at whereby the Grand Trunk would acknowledge their obligations in respect of the Grand Trunk Pacific or be relieved of them.
