Mr. Chairman, with regard to the public ownership of railways, the point that I am most particularly interested in is the policy of the Government with regard to the management of the road. Reading again from the Drayton-Acworth report, I find this:
The railway touches the life of the country at innumerable points. It can almost make one city and unmake another. It vitally affects the question whether an Industry in one place Is more or less profitable than in another. Every city wants to become a railway centre, to have railway works located within its limits. And the local member invariably wants it too. Every citizen wants the railway station placed where it best suits his own personal convenience, and wants that every express train shall sto-j at it.

I have in mind a case which I think will apply to this condition. The Canadian Northern had at Calgary some twenty or twenty-five engines operating from Calgary on the Goose Lake line. The company transferred them to Hanna for some unknown reason. They also transferred some seventy-five employees of the road. They took them from Calgary where they had every convenience as regards water supply, coal facilities and facilities for the men, and transferred them to Hanna where they are hauling water some fifty miles to supply the engines. There may be a sufficient reason for this transfer there, but it is not apparent to the people along the line. It seems to be an additional cost to the service; and it might account for some of the figures which I have quoted of the earnings and expenditures in connection with the running of the road since the Government took it over. I am not opposed to public ownership of railways, although there has never resulted any great success from such ownership, principally for the reason that the roads are always brought into politics; and if the great railway systems of this country are to become a political football and a patronage outlet for the Government we shall undoubtedly lose a lot of money. It has cost a great deal more to run the Canadian Northern this year, than before the Government took it over, and no doubt it will take more to run the Grand Trunk Pacific. The Drayton-Acworth report specifically says that it will under no consideration recommend railways to be taken over and managed by the Government, and suggests that there should be a commission appointed, and this seems quite reasonable. There are a great number of people in this country who are very anxious to have public ownership, but apparently there are very few who are giving any attention to the question of management. I fear that we will be confronted with difficulties, after we have expended a lot of money, and find ourselves in deeper water in this railway problem. We had an instance in the Railway Committee the other day. The Grand Trunk were asking to be allowed to sell some more securities, many of the members of the committee objecting strenuously. Some other promoter had a railway starting from nowhere in particular and ending anywhere, and there did not seem to be an objection to his getting an extension of time. There are some one hundred or one hundred and fifty railways projected by promoters who hope at some future time to unload them on the Dominion of Canada; and just as soon as these railroads
are allowed to pass the Railway Committee, get a charter, and get organized, and sell their securities, and get a subsidy from the Dominion Government, there will be difficulties. I think the whole question should be seriously considered by the Government and the entire system worked out on some basis of public and private ownership. It seems to me that the ideal condition would be to have our present public-owned railways properly managed and leave the Canadian Pacific railway as it is. I think the Canadian National railway might form a working arrangement with the Grand Trunk that would save the country from taking over that end of it. A traffic arrangement might surely be made with them. They need the outlet in the West, just as much as the western lines need the outlet in the East; and there might be some arrangement by which the Grand Trunk and the Government railways could co-operate. They would have as competitor the Canadian Pacific railway. We would then have a private-owned road and a Government-owned road, and we could test the two plans and ascertain which is the better. But apparently the Government has given this matter no thought whatever. The Prime Minister at the last session said that it was his intention that there should be a commission, and that this matter should be taken as far as possible out of politics. Since that time, however, we find that ten new directors of the Canadian National railway have been appointed, and I have been unable to find any special reason for their appointment. So far as I can learn they had no qualifications to recommend them as railroad men. This undertaking is a large one. It embraces some 15,000 miles of railway and something over a billion dollars of investment, and should therefore surely merit the most earnest consideration of the Government. The whole problem must be carefully worked out if the situation is to be saved. There can be no advantage in taking over these railroads if the cost of operation will be more than at the present time. The people of the Dominion must pay the charges no matter whether the railways are privately or publicly owned. If the Grand Trunk Pacific as a company system cost only $7,000,000 of the people's money to run, and it would cost $10,000,000 as a public-owned proposition, we would be losing some millions. It cannot be an asset if it is a losing proposition, and it would be just as well to leave it as it is; and until we realize the importance of the management and work out a system whereby

we shall get the best possible results, we shall continue to lose money. I fail to understand why a grocer, and a broker, and a steel magnate, should be directors of a railway system; and I think that we might follow the Drayton-Acworth report and appoint the best railway men we could get in Canada, giving them a free hand and paying them good salaries. I think also it will be necessary to adopt some system of co-operation with the employees of the road, some profit-sharing system, in order that we may obtain the best service from the employees. As things are at present, under political management, they are uncertain as to the future. There may be changes of government, of management and of directors, and, naturally changes of employees, unless we can take these roads out . of politics. The question of the extensions of the railroads should also be taken into serious consideration. There are places where the railroads must be extended, and there are places where we have too many roads already; and that question should be dealt with by some other body of impartial men who would not be at the beck and call of a member for any district. A road may be needed for the development of territory where it will not yield interest charges and operating expenses at first. There should be some system by which such a road could be subsidized to a certain extent, after it had been passed upon by some independent body. We should also establish the capitalization of these roads. We have the Intercolonial without capitalization, and the Canadian Northern with heavy capitalization. We should establish the capitalization on which roads within a reasonable period of years would be in a position to earn money. Hand the roads over to a commission and let them state to the Government, if you will, what they expect to require in the way of cash assistance from this country in order to put them in good shape, and what they expect to require before they can be made to pay, and how long they expect to operate before getting any returns. If we go on in our present haphazard way, however, reaching out and taking a railway here and another there, we shall certainly have difficulties. The last night of last session, about ten o'clock at night, there was brought uip the question of some four or five railroads. The Minister of Railways and Canals (Mr. J. D. Reid), a great public ownership man, turned to his friend, the Minister of Public Works (Mr. Carvell), who was more or less of a private-ownership man, and with their 
co-operation we gobbled up four or five railroads.
I do not know how much work has been done on them since, nor what system has been adopted to put them into shape. The railway situation will never work itself out until we adopt a policy of colonization to get people along the lines of road and to get the land that is being held out of use into such a condition that people can go and settle upon it and produce traffic for the railways.

Mr. Chairman, I have listened with a great deal of interest to the hon. the member for Pontiac (Mr. Cahill) but I cannot agree with him. I am an absolute believer in the public ownership of railways in this country. I came into this House on that doctrine. I have seen it expand and grow and take possession of the hearts of the people. The people are determined that the old system must end forever and a new system take its place. That new system is public ownership. One of the first war measures of the Mother Country was to take over the railways of Great Britain. They will never part with them. The United States have taken over the railways. They have had difficulties, but they are trying to surmount them. They are co-ordinating the roads, they are licking them into shape, and while they have not made any profits, and people say it has 'been expensive to run them, the real fact is that the roads had been allowed to run down and they required immense expenditures to restore them to a profitable basis.
The people of the United States have justified that expenditure. They have a body in the United States called the Council of Agriculture. That council, represented by its chairman and prominent members, waited upon the Senate Committee, discussing the railway situation, and said: We come here representing the farmers of the United States who, in their organized capacity, are in favour of public ownership and who believe that this is the only way of getting substantial relief from their transportation difficulties. They are going to continue public ownership in the United States. They have it, as a matter of fact, in England although there is some legislating yet to do. Germany held her predominence in the war largely because of her state-owned railways, all Europe has been converted to state-owned railways and no country there proposes to abandon the principle of state ownership.
We believe in it in the province of Ontario. I have watched closely the develop-

ment of public opinion on that question,
1 know what the people there are thinking and I have no hesitation in saying that they are in favour of public ownership. We have a provincially-owned railway. It is doing good work, it is well administered and it has opened up a new portion of the country. While it has not paid any dividends yet, it is a splendid asset for the province. We have also another fine example of public ownership in the Hydroelectric system of Ontario, which supplies the people with heat, light and power. They have made a great success of it there, and they are going to extend it to local radial railways.
I was up in the West taking part in a little campaign on that question. Those who fought the idea of public ownership in connection with the radial system were not in it when the votes were counted. The workmen and farmers in Ontario are all for public ownership when they are asked to pronounce upon local proposals of that kind. When the next election comes around the people will demand by their votes that we shall have a well-established system of public ownership. So far we have had to take the lean ends, the failures, and the roads that have been exploited by capitalists of all kinds. After the capitalists and contractors have made fortunes for themselves, and the public have spent immense sums of money, the people are compelled to come along to recover these roads and take them over.
What have we paid for this whole adventure in connection with the Grand Trunk Pacific? Not less than half a million dollars-1500,000,000 has gone into this railway proposition extending from the Atlantic to the Pacific. Then, when we take it over, we will have to pay $25,000,000 a year, which means $5 for every man, woman and child in this country, notwithstanding what we have already spent on the road. It has not been organized, it is not serving the people, although the money has been paid out. Somebody has got a lot of money, but we have to pay for it. We not only had to pay for it the first time, but now we have to take it over and do the best we can. There must be no more of that kind of thing. If any one comes into this House while I am a member of it and tries to get the people's money paid out for the construction of a railway, which railway will sooner or later be dumped on the public to be taken care of by them, I am not going to vote for it. Nor will I ever vote for another dollar of public money for any privately-owned railway.
They talk about the public not being able to administer a railway. Was there ever such incompetency in the history of the world as that which has been disclosed by the record of the railways in the United States and Canada under the management of private companies? Nearly every one of these roads has become bankrupt? Nearly every one has gone through the profits, has failed, and the people who put their money into them have been looted and ruined by the so-called executives of these railways. The public have never been served. Competition never did anything for the public, but the money was spent. The exploiters had control. They did the contracting in one way and another, with the result that the roads have been wrecked. The net result on the American continent is that private ownership has wrecked the railway systems of United States and Canada, with the single exception of the Canadian Pacific.
My opinion is that the people of Canada have determined that there shall be no more exploitation of the public in this respect, and ieast of all are they prepared to take the advice of the hon. member for Pontiac, who says: Appoint another commission and allow this thing to continue; let us find out what we can do. The thing is to do something now.
The hon. gentleman is misquoting me. I said: Appoint a commission to manage the present Canadian National Railways instead of the liovernment managing them.

I know that the hon. gentleman is no advocate of the proposition before the Govefnment. But, we have to deal with this question now. We cannot go out, get information and appoint a commission; we have to deal with the facts before us. Here is a great railway system in default. The Government and Parliament must deal with it, and the Government have come forward with a proposition. My only criticism is that they are not going far enough. When we are winding up the Grand Trunk Pacific is the time to wind up the old Grand Trunk. Perhaps that will come in a few days. That, I expect, will be the result of the provision which is being made now. I also agree with the hon. the Acting Prime Minister (Sir Thomas White) when he says it is up to the Grand Trunk to say something and do something now. The next move is theirs.
But in the meantime we are going to put an end to all this exploitation in connection with the old Grand Trunk Pacific. We will take it over if we have to. We will join it



up with the Canadian Northern, and will take over the ragged ends. As I said before, if we take the Grand Trunk Pacific we want the old Grand Trunk, which, if joined up to the Intercolonial, the Grand Trunk Pacific, the Transcontinental and the other roads that we have taken over, will make a Canadian national system which can be linked together and co-ordinated, and all unnecessary trackage perhaps thrown out. If that is done a great saving can be made. When we begin to do things like that we will really have public ownership, and we will find people in this country who can administer railroads. The people of this country will stand no longer for an administration of the public railways being made a part of a political machine-the day for all that has gone by. They administer the railways in England without politics, and for the time the Government had them they did so in the United States under the administration of Mr. McAdoo. There was not much politics in connection with the administration of the railways there, and there will be no politics in the administration of the railays in this country: we will find the men who will administer our railways properly.

How does the hon.
member propose to have responsible government, and yet have the management of the railroads not responsible to Parliament?	.

I do not think
there is much in that point. We will have the railways administered by public ownership, perhaps by commission. Parliament must take the responsibility, under our system of government, eventually, but that does n,ot mean that there will be any interference with the men who are administering the railways. I will undertake to find people in this country-any one would undertake to do so-who can run these roads. What a pitiable situation it is to se in this country the railroads already in existence -the combinations that are in existence (and they are always conspiring) [DOT] they want to see public ownership defeated. That great system, the Canadian Pacific, which has been a success, what is it doing to-day? It is doing its best to prevent the Government from getting hold of the Grand Trunk. It does not want to see a success made of a national system of railways, for it knows that is coming and that it will be here in a very short time.
I approve of this Act of the Government in dealing with the Grand Trunk Pacific, but I think it must be followed a little later on by taking over the Grand Trunk and

consolidating it with the railroads we now have. I would be prepared now, and I believe the people of Canada largely would be prepared, to take over the Canadian Pacific and give it a reasonable arrangement whereby we would have one national system. We are a poor nation, Mr. Speaker, after what we have done from a national point of view-from the point of view of fighting, and one thing or another

if we cannot run our own railroads in the interest of the public. I hate to hear men in public life talking about putting the administration of our railroads into the hands of politicians. I propose to put them into the hands of Canadians, I propose to have them take the administration of the roads and make a success of it. It has been made a success in Australia, in New Zealand, all over the continent of Europe, and the British Government are doing it all over Africa. India has national railroads, France has national railroads, and there is not a country which is preparing to depart from that principle. They are all coming to it, and we are coming to it-we have arrived at it. Here in Canada the people are in favour of it, and I hope it will not be long before we have, not only the Grand Trunk Pacific, but the Grand Trunk proper, in our national railway system.
Now who is it that objects to taking over this Grand Trunk 'adventure, after the _en-ormous expenditure in connection with it? You will always find there are three interests in connection with railroads. First of all there is the public that is served; then there are the people who have their money invested-the shareholders or the investors-and there are always another clever lot who have the executive power in their hands. And that comes home to the men in London who have been administering the Grand Trunk for a great many years. They do not care for the public, or for the 'shareholders; they have been exploiting the shares of the Grand Trunk in its various forms for fifty years in the London market; and they would like to keep that power as long as they can, they would like to dabble in Grand Trunk securities, and they would like to have the patronage and the handing out of the contracts in connection with the Grand Trunk. Therefore I do not take any stock in this objection to public ownership of railways that comes from the executive of the Grand Trunk. I would make this suggestion to the Government: If it wishes to make this campaign effective, the first thing it should do is get a list of the shareholders of the Grand Trunk and send them a copy of this debate, and let the shareholders of the

Grand Trunk know what has been concealed from them, so far as I can gather-that is the actual commitments to which those shareholders have been pledged by this, so-called, executive in London. How many of them know what this country has already paid for that road-what we have paid on their account, and what commitments and obligations they have failed to perform? They do not know it. Instead of that the shareholders of the Grand Trunk in England have been told that in some way the people of Canada are robbers, that we are confiscating their property. All we have asked the company to do is to make good their undertakings. Why do they not make good their undertakings? We loaned them money, and the credit to build the Grand Trunk Pacific. The money has been spent and the roads are there, but the steel is rusting, and the farmers want the service which these railways should provide. Let us give them that service. Let us help to open Quebec and Northern Ontario with this great transcontinental system. How many millions were put into the Quebec bridge? Was it thirty millions? And the expenditure is not yet over. That is an adventure, that was not done by public ownership-that is an adventure of private ownership connected with politics. That has all got to stop. Now that we have paid the money and got these roads, we should tell these men who have made a mess of things to step down and out, and let the people run these railways.
Could there have been a worse mess than the Grand Trunk magnates in London have landed this great Grand Trunk Pacific railway into? I have heard what the late Sir Wilfrid Laurier said some time ago with respect to that scheme in which he took so much interest. I saw him introduce the project into this House, and I have followed it from its inception to the end. Apparently Sir Wilfrid put his faith in one individual, in Mr. Hays, for the carrying of it out, and when Mr. Hays died, Sir Wilfrid said it would have a bad effect on the fortunes and the future of the road. But whether that be so or not the fact remains that the people of Canada put half a billion of money into this one proposition. They put up the money, they signed the agreements, and yet these magnates in London, who made those solemn agreements, are dodging the responsibility, are trying to evade it-they want to leave the baby on the doorstep of the people of Canada. Now there is to be no more of that in connection with our railroads. We will 434
take them over, we will try and run them, and we will put these railroads on their feet.
On wheels.

Very well, on * wheels-and we will make them serve the people, but we want no more adjournment of the matter, and no opportunity given to the Grand Trunk to continue its plotting.
Now here is what is going on in Montreal largely: The great thing that I read in the papers there is that in some way we should not wreck this poor old Grand Trunk and we should not confiscate this property. While that argument is advanced, two things are going on: First, the Canadian Pacific has been trying for months to get control of the old Grand Trunk. I do not think anybody will deny that. The other thing that has been observed going on is that - the Canadian Pacific would like to see delay in the nationalization of the railways, they would like to see it fail, and they would like to see Canada loaded up with the poor ends like the Canadian Northern, the Intercolonial, possibly, and the Transcontinental, which some people say goes through a wilderness. But now that we have paid this money, give us one good railroad in Ontario, where the main mileage of the old Grand Trunk is to be found, and let the people run it. If you do, it will be a success; it will help to carry the other roads along, and you will have a good national system of railways.
I have heard the grievances of the farmers in connection with the tariff. I have studied the tariff question, and I have studied also the transportation question. You can give real relief to the people of the West, you can settle up that part of our country, you can bring about lower freight rates, by the establishing of a national -system of railways better than you can in any other way. And we must also own a national system of transportation on the sea; we are cdming to that. Every time the railway commission get a reduction of freight rates for the farmers, the men who control our steamship services, especially the Englishmen, who have no special regard for this country, jump up the ocean transport charges. We do not get the benefit of reduced freight rates or of the money that we vote to secure railway competition. But when we have a national system of railways devoted to serving our people, opening up settlement and reducing the rates of transportation, our country will go ahead. If the mem-

That, I think, sufficiently refutes the position taken by the hon. member for Pontiac. Then he says: Who is responsible for the railway situation in Canada to-day? I do not know that it very much matters who is responsible. The railways in Canada, like the poor, we always have with us; but there is one thing perfectly certain, and that is that neither the Unionist party nor the Conservative party were in power in 1903, when the contract between the Grand Trunk 'Railway Company and the Dominion of Canada was made that led us into the difficulty in which we find ourselves. Nor were the Conservative party in power in 1911, when the Canadian Northern Railway system, by a subsidy granted by the then Minister of Railways, Hon. George P. Graham, was permitted to leave the Western Provinces >
and get an eastern connection, and to take the first step towards making what had been a local railway system into a transcontinental railway system. But I want to be just; I do not want to endeavour to place the responsibility altogether on hon. gentlemen opposite, because if they were responsible in 1903 and again in 1911, there is one thing quite sure, namely, that the Conservative Government of later years were, in my judgment, responsible when they permitted the Canadian Northern Railway system to be extended from Winnipeg to the coast, because it was a national crime to allow the parallelling of the Canadian Pacific from Kamloops to the Pacific coast along one side of the Fraser and Thompson rivers while the Canadian Pacific ran down the other side. But who were to blame? We were all to blame, because the people of Canada allowed themselves to be bribed with their own money. We were to blame because the people of Canada were led to believe that this railway expenditure and development were going to make good times, and the majority, or a great number of the people of Canada thought there was going to be something in it for them. The people allowed themselves to be bribed with their own money, and fate brought them to punishment, and we are paying to-day for our irregularity and our weakness of a few years ago.
The construction of the Grand Trunk Pacific brought great industrial activity in

Canada; the recognition by the Government of 1911 of the right of the Canadian Northern to become a transcontinental railway brought further great development, and between them we had competition in expenditures. Wages rose and the cost of materials rose. Instead of the Grand Trunk Pacific and the National Transcontinental being built at the estimated cost of those who had launched the schemes, prices .were greatly enhanced. The original estimate of the National Transcontinental was about $61,000,000. The real cost was approximately $160,000,000, $99,000,000 over the estimate, or 150 per cent.
The Grand Trunk Railway engineers had the right to draw the specifications, they had the right to supervise and the right to inspect, and yet this country in the inauguration of a public-owned system of railways is burdened down with part of a national transcontinental railway at a cost of $99,000,000 beyond what it should have cost. Now, Sir, I have said that the inflation and the competition between the two railroads tremendously increased the cost, and the members of this House have a right to ask: "How does he know it? Why does he say it? Is it a fact? Can he prove it?" I think those are fair questions, and I want to prove it, not by any isolated fact that I might produce of my own knowledge, but out of the mouth of Mr. Chamberlin himself. There is one unfortunate thing when a man takes an oath and swears to tell the truth-that is, unfortunate, possibly, from his point of view when the evidence turns against him -and that is he has no reason to complain when the people believe him and have reason to suppose that what he said was a fact. What did Mr. Chamberlin of the Grand Trunk Railway Company say when he was giving evidence before the Drayton-Acworth-Smith Commission in Montreal on the 24th February, 1917, as to the cost of the Canadian Northern, the Grand Trunk Pacific and the National Transcontinental? He said-Page 82:
Mr. Chamberlin: In the first place, all our estimates were made on the basis of $1.50 for labour, $1.75 to make it safe. Labour is the principal part of the construction of a railway. The result was that with the other road working right alongside of us, especially west of Edmonton, we had to pay $3.50 a day right along, and even then the men would not work. If we tried to crowd them and make them work, they would simply climb over the fence, so to speak, and go to work for the Canadian Northern.
Sir Henry Drayton: But your position would be no worse in that respect than that of the Canadian Northern.

Mr. Chamberlin: Not in that respect. Still, it tremendously increased the cost of the road. In addition to that, all material was increased in price. The Canadian Pacific Railway was constructing feverishly all the time to keep up with the other two. That increased the cost of material away beyond any expectations. There were also duties put on everything after that contract was made-
That is the contract for the construction of the two roads.
-such as $7 a ton on rails. So you see everything counted.
Tnat simply goes to prove that the construction of those two roads at the one time created an inflation, increased prices, and made the cost infinitely more expensive than had originally been estimated
But the hon. member for Pontiac st.ll seems to be willing to excuse tl e Grand Trunk. As I said, I want to be fair. I want to view this thing as if I were to an extent a shareholder in the Grand Trunk Railway Company. As a shareholder in the railroad I should feel myself estopped by the conduct of my management, and although I had made a loss I do not believe I should be justified in saying that what the management had done and what I as a shareholder had approved, I now had a right to claim to be freed from. When the Grand Trunk came to the Government of this country-I want to emphasize this point: the Government of the day, Sir Wilfrid Laurier's Government, did not go to the Grand Trunk and ask them to build this railroad, but the Grand Trunk came to the Government of Sir Wilfrid Laurier and endeavoured to enter into a contract to. permit of the building of the National Transcontinental and the Grand Trunk Pacific, because the Grand Trunk Railway wanted a western outlet, wanted a long haul and a western connection-when the Grand Trunk came to the Government they asked the Government only for a railroad from North Bay westward. That was a sound policy and probably if that arrangement as contemplated by the Grand Trunk had been adhered to, the difficulties we have had to _ contend with in this country might not have arisen. But the Government of the day-and I say it advisedly, because I think history will prove it, and certainly the facts will not disprove it-the Government of the day, and the members of the Parliament of that day, for political reasons insisted that the arrangement as contemplated should not be carried out, and they insisted on the construction of a railway away down through the northern part of this country and across the Maritime Provinces to Moncton. They loaded the Grand Trunk down with a load
it could never hope to carry, but the Grand Trunk knew before they signed the contract what the contract was to be, and I do not see how it lies in the mouth of the Grand Trunk Railway to come to this country now and say that we are .hard and unreasonable when we ask them to live up to the contract they made. And the Grand Trunk do admit that the contract they are asked to live up to is a contract that cannot be lived up to. You ask me why I do say this. I again turn to the sworn evidence of Mr. Chamberlin at Montreal-page 79. Mr. Chamberlin had been giving evidence as to why the Grand Trunk should not he asked to live up to its obligations, and after he had given his first reason Sir Henry Drayton said to him:
Sir Henry Drayton: Tour second ground is that of impossibility?
Mr. Chamberlin: It is an impossibility.
Sir Henry Drayton: If it is impossible now, it was always impossible.
Mr. Chamberlin: It was always impossible.
In other words, the Grand Trunk Railway Company entered into a contract with the Government of this country which Mr. Chamberlin says was always impossible for that railroad to carry out.
What reason has the Grand Trunk Railway to come to us and ask to be relieved of "its obligations? What reason has the Grand Trunk Railway to come to this country, which has done much more for the Grand Trunk Railway than we ever promised lu do, and say: "You arc treating us harshly. Relieve us from our obligations."
You listened this afternoon, -Sir, to the very excellent summary of the Acting Prime Minister, and what did it show?
