Now, Sir, to put that into short metre, it means this: That we have given the Grand Trunk and the Grand Trunk Pacific railway, by loans and guarantees, $63,000,000 more than we promised them. We have taken over the National Transcontinental, which stands this country at $161,000,000,-$99,000,000 more than it was estimated the National Transcontinental would cost,'-and the Drayton and Acworth report says $50,000,000 is required to put the Grand Trunk Railway system in adequate operation and so maintain is as to give satisfactory service to Canada. And yet the member for Pontiac (Mr. Cahill) hesitated this afternoon in saying that the time had come when Canada should act, not only to save her credit, but also to secure an adequate railway system for this country. I do not believe that is the opinion of the people of Canada. If I can read aright the policies we hear enunciated from the Atlantic to the Pacific, it i3 that the time has come when Canada is to cease subsidizing railroads, that we are going to own what we pay for. If we have got

to pay the costs in any event, then we are going to have the profits if there are profits. But just here, Sir, I would	like
pause to make one remark. I said if there are profits we are going to have the profits. But as a Government-ownership man I want to have a fair chance, I want unnecessary paralleling of lines eliminated, I want the whole of the system co-ordinated, and I do want the additional capital that has been absorbed by these .undertakings through improper construction, fraudulent specifications, inadequate checking, and all that we summarize in the cost of irregular and irrelevant construction, eliminated from what I might call the capital charges against the venture. I do not want the Canadian national system of railroads loaded up with the interest on $100,000,000 of overhead charge through the unfortunate cqst of construction of the National Transcontinental. I do not want the system loaded up with all the cost of paralleling lines that never should have been built. Government ownership in this country must get a fair show, and then it must stand or fall on its merits. But if it is to have a fair show, there must, as I said, be co-ordination of the various lines, there must be an elimination of waste in management, there must be the squeezing out of all the water represented by improper, and, as I said, irregular construction and flotation.
Somebody has said that you cannot have government operation and administration oi railroads, because you cannot get men to run them honestly. I may be an idealist, I may look forward to Utopia, hut in the eleven years I have been in public life there is one thing that I have learned, and that is that we are making a tremendous advance along the line of the willingness of big men to do public service. When the war broke out we saw men for an ideal go to the Front, willing to sacrifice their lives for $1.10 a day,-I was going to say, remuneration. No, they did not go to the Front to sacrifice their lives for $1.10 a day; they went to the Front moved by that enthusiasm which makes men realize that to die for one's country is sweet; and I believe, Sir, that the aftermath of this war will bring Canadians to realize that if it is dear and sweet for a man to die for his country, it is equally sweet for a man to live for his country. And I believe the time is coming, if the time is not already here, .when great men may be had in Canada to run our national railway system. Not great business men, simply because they have succeeded in a business that is not

a railroad, but great men. who have mastered a railroad system, great men who understand railway operation, experts in railway administration. I may say, Sir, that I agree with the hon. member for Pontiac that the present system is a long way from being ideal. I would no more think of, taking a grocer' and asking him to run a dry goods store, than I would think of taking a man from managing a steel plant or running a cement works, and asking him to run a railroad. What I should like to see this country do is to take over the Grand Trunk Pacific-we have already the Intercolonial, Transcontinental and the Canadian Northern systems- take over the old Grand Trunk-because it is insolvent and cannot finance itself-press the water out of the system, get the best railway men that the country can produce; and if Canada cannot produce the men let us get them from England or the United States, but let us secure the very best men we can get. Let us have a railroad system owned by this country and operated by independent, courageous men, and let us demonstrate to the world that Canada can do, and successfully do, that which she determines to do well.

I would like to make one or two comments on the railway situation as it has developed out of the resolution before the House. First of all, I would congratulate the Acting Prime Minister and the Government on the resolute action they took when the Grand Trunk put them with their backs against the wall, so to speak, with their ultimatum that the Grand Trunk Pacific would stop operating at 1 a.m. on the 10th instant. Speaking in this House last Session I put on Hansard a set of figures with regard to the National Transcontinental, the Grand Trunk Pacific and the Grand Trunk Railway of Canada, that so far have not either been contradicted or disproved. I pointed out at that time-I am not going to weary the House with the details, any one who wishes can find the figures on Hansard-that through the construction of the National Transcontinental and the Grand Trunk Pacific railways, for all of which the Grand Trunk Railway Company of Canada was either directly or contingently liable, and for all of which the people . of Canada were either directly or contingently liable, $260,000,000 had gone into something that was not the construction of a railway. We are not going to get anywhere if we start in to throw bricks at each other as to who is responsible for that, but the fact remains that $260,-
000,000-not $100,000,000, as any hon. friend has told us on the National Transcontinental east of Winnipeg, but $120,000,000 on the National Transcontinental east of Winnipeg, and $130,000,000 on the Grand Trunk Pacific west of Winnipeg-went into something that was not the construction of railways. That was not due to any wrong estimate, or to any increase in the wages paid to workmen, or the cost of steel or anything else, but was deliberately applied to some other purpose. In support of that statement, take the construction of the Canadian Northern, which was carried on side by side with it, and you will find, by simply estimating, the value of the physical assets of each, that what I say is absolutely correct. Now the point is simply this: As has been emphasized-and I think it should be re-emphasized in order that the people of this country may not be misunderstood by those who have put their money into the Grand Trunk Railway Company, or by English or European investors who may have put or or may hereafter put their money into any industry in Canada-the Canadian people are not responsible for anything more than they did themselves on the National Transcontinental east of Winnipeg. Let me repeat again what I said in this House last year, that if the Canadian people are willing to assume the responsibility for what they themselves threw away east of Winnipeg, there is no logical reason why the Grand Trunk Railway of Canada should not be responsible for what their officers threw away on the construction west of Winnipeg.
I agree with the Acting Prime Minister that we should be reasonably generous, but I do not agree that we should be generous to the point that has been suggested. It is not a difficult matter to estimate the value of a railway. It is just as easy for a railway man to determine whaJt a railway is worth as it is for a builder to determine what a building is worth. All you have to do is to measure the railway, take stock of its physical condition, the number of locomotives and cars of all descriptions it has, and you can determine its value without the least bit of trouble. Not what it cost. If you are going to build a house you are not going to ask the owner how much money he has sunk in schemes of architecture, but you will endeavour to find out what the value of the building is.
A railway is simply worth its mileage valuation, assuming that it was properly projected and reasonably constructed. And that is the situation with regard to the

Grand Trunk Railway system. But, that we have to take it over and assume responsibility for it has become evident to everyone who has studied the railway situation ever since we became loaded up with the Transcontinental and the Grand Trunk Pacific. Now that we are going to do it, as the member for Kingston (Mr. Nickle) has said, let us do it in such a way that there will be reasonable probability of our making the thing a success. I said last year in this House-and I was questioned very pertinently from both sides in this regard- that we should squeeze the water out of the Grand Trunk, the Grand Trunk Pacific, the National Transcontinental. And somebody must squeeze $750,000,000 out of the capitalization, as given to us by the officers themselves, of the Grand Trunk Railway system. The figures may be found in the DraytonTAcworth report.
You will find in that report that the president of the Grand Trunk Railway Company, Mr. Chamberlin, was asked specifically by Sir Henry Drayton during the course of his examination why it was that during the number of years when, by his own statement, the railway was depreciating in value, a large sum of money had been paid out in dividends, and why that money had not been used to keep the rolling stock and locomotives, the general physical condition of the road, as it ought to be. In effect, Mr. Chamberlin's answer was this: We were contemplating going on the London market with a block of bonds in connection with putting in a further amount of capital, and in order to stabilize that market we wanted to have a good record in the payment of dividends; in other words, we wanted to pay to ourselves annually over a number of years money that should have gone into the road, in order that we might induce the public to think that this was a good investment and that they should buy our bonds. If any one of us did that, we would find ourselves behind prison bars within a very short time. But that is what the president of the Grand Trunk Railway Company of Canada said his company did instead of putting the money into ties, rails, locomotives, cars, and everything else that was necessary to keep the road operating. However, we are faced, not with a theory, but with an actual situation. The Grand Trunk Railway Company have come to the point where they say they cannot carry their obligation any further and are going to stop operating the Grand Trunk Pacific, a part of their own system that they themselves brought into existence; and that we may

take it or leave it, as we like. In the most direct way possible, the Government of Canada should take the Grand Trunk Railway system at their word, acquire the property, co-ordinate it as quickly as possible and get rid of all unnecessary lines. Certain lines of railway in Canada are built side by side with other lines. We might as well make up our minds to tear them up. I have heard people say: " Why, that piece of railway cost ten, fifteen, or twenty millions." Suppose it did; if we can get three or four millions out of the rails or make use of them somewhere else where they are really required, why should we continue to operate lines of railway where they never could earn anything and where the country through which they run is already amply served? I told the Minister of Railways in this House last year that I could show him where he could get $10,000,000 worth of steel rails that will never earn money enough to keep the rust off them; that run parallel with other lines which serve all the purposes for which a railway was ever designed. It looks like bad housekeeping on our part, but we went into these things with our eyes wide open, and we have to take our medicine. Whether it looks well or whether it does not, action will have to be taken if we are to co-ordinate this national system of railways and make it a complete success.
Some of the things that I have said in this House may have led hon. members to think that I am an out-and-out advocate of the public ownership of railways. In that respect I disagree with the two hon. members who have preceded me. If some one could show us a method by which we could get out of the tangle in which we find ourselves and get back into the position we were in fifteen or twenty years ago, I would hold up both hands for it. The only reason why I support the idea of taking over these lines and co-ordinating them into one national system is because I cannot see any other way out. It is a tremendous problem to take these railways and put them into such a condition that they can be successfully operated. Notwithstanding all that ha!s been said with regard to the large number of men who can be found whose ideals of service will cause them to give their time efficiently and conscientiously to the public, and all that kind of thing, I submit that human nature is human nature and will continue to be so. So far as I can see, the one bright spot in the horizon is the presence in Canada of one complete, well-equipped and splen-

didly managed system of railways. The possibility of success lies in linking up all the other lines and operating them in competition with that efficient system, saying to the men whom we put in charge: Here is your line of railways capitalized at not a dollar more than the one you are competing with; your physical conditions are on the same plane; you can bring the mileage of the national railways up to exactly the same cost value as the Canadian Pacific railway by eliminating the results of wasteful expenditure; simply look upon the sums of which this country has been virtually robbed as money that we spent while on a spree, so to speak; and charge the railways up to what they should have cost, approximately $65,000 a mile, brought up to 100 per cent efficiency. If we do that, appoint a Board of Management of practical men and operate the national railways in competition with a system that is run on practical lines, there is, I believe, a possibility of success. Then, these railways, instead of being a continually recurring burden, will earn their own way and give the people what they are looking for-service.
The member for Kingston (Mr. Nickle) referred to the success of Government ownership of railways in all parts of the world. If he will take the trouble to investigate he will find that in no country under the sun, except in the United States, is a.ton of freight carried a mile as cheaply as it is in Canada. The Australian system of publicly-owned railways has been held up to the world as a model, but for twenty years it has cost two and a half times as much to move a ton of freight a mile on the railways in Australia as it has cost on Canadian railways. The effort made in the United States by the Government to coordinate all their railways has been referred to as a great success.
It was not so much of a success last year when boats were held up in the harbour of New York for ten days at a time, when the railways could not get coal in there for them. It was not even a success from the standpoint of operation. The very first thing the United States Government did when they undertook to co-ordinate the railways of that country was to do the very thing they had been refusing permission to the railway companies to do themselves. The United States had been developing a policy that made it utterly impossible for one railway to assist another in the movement of its traffic, it mattered not what the conditions were. But apart altogether from that, the operation of the United States railways in 1918, when one takes into consideration the excess freight rates and the deficit involved, cost about $1,250,000,000, and the co-relative effect of that is that every man, woman and child in the Dominion of Canada is paying, in the year 1919, $9 for freight and railway services more than they were paying before. We are. however, talking simply along theoretical lines. We might discuss this matter all night and we would never get the Grand Trunk and the Grand Trunk Pacific off the backs of the people of Canada. Our business is to put these railways in such a condition that they can operate successfully in competition with the best managed and best equipped railway under the sun to-day, namely the Canadian Pacific, the one railway system in the whole civilised world that never broke down during the whole period of the war through which we have passed. Had it not been for the service which that railway company, privately owned and managed, rendered, this country would not have been able to do the big things we did in this great war.
May I repeat:	We should get a Board
of Management-I do not care what you call it; I do not like the present arrangement in connection with the Canadian National railways. I do not like the name. Instead of making the Canadian Northern a part of the Canadian National railways, we have made the Canadian National railways a part of the Canadian Northern. I would call the system the National Railways of Canada. I do not like the 'Canadian Northern mixed up in it at all. Do not misunderstand me in connection with that. When the Canadian people got the Canadian Northern at the valuation at which they got it, they got the cheapest railway ever built on the North American continent, mile for mile and dollar for dollar. The Canadian people can spend $190,000,000 on the Canadian Northern, on improvement of the roadbed, construction of terminals, purchase of rolling stock and all the things that go to make up a standard railway, and they will have it on the same valuation as the Canadian Pacific.
Mr. LEMiIEUX:	Was it the valuation
of the Drayton-Acworth report?
(Mr. G. B. NIGHOLiSON: I do not know anything about the valuation of the Drayton-Acworth report. I am speaking about the value of the railway. Take the railway as it is; you can spend $190,000,000 on it and my hon. friend, if he will look up Hansard of last year, will find that there is a margin of $50,000,000 for contingencies over and above the estimate required to

bring that railway up to 100 per cent efficiency, which $50,000,000 we may never have to spend. If we do spend it, we shall have $190,000,000 over and above what was paid for the railway, every dollar of which is to link that up with the other system, co-ordinating them properly, eliminating the waste mileage and putting them under proper management. In that way we .shall be able to complete the system and give the people the service for which they are asking.
Let me say this final word to the Government : Get busy and do this just as quickly as you can. There is no problem facing the people of this country in a physical sense that is so vital as the railway problem. We got into it with our eyes open; now let us get out of it. The country will be able to carry the burden and the railway will give us good service.
Mr. J. A. ROBB (Chateauguay-Hunting-don); The debate this afternoon has developed the idea that it is the policy of the Government to have public ownership of the railways as soon as possible. The Acting Prime Minister, in presenting his case so well as he is able to present it, made the admission that negotiations for the ownership of the Grand Trunk Hailway, not the Grand Trunk Pacific Railway, were started by the Government in a communication to Mr. Smithers. It is, therefore, quite apparent that the Government, having acquired the Canadian Northern Railway, which turns out unprofitable, now find it necessary to acquire the old Grand Trunk Railway in an effort to make the Canadian Northern pay. I take it that the Government are not unanimous upon this question. No later than last summer, the Minister of Public Works (Mr. Carvell), speaking before the Canadian Club in Montreal, left the impression with the business men of that city, that the Government were not favourable to public ownership. It seems to me that the House and the country are entitled to some better reason than -has been presented this afternoon as to why this change of policy occurred. The Minister of Public Works comes from a province where the people have had many years' experience of Government-owned and operated railways, and his statement of the case was that Government ownership was disastrous to the country. We all know that the Maritime Provinces have suffered from Government ownership. Those rich provinces have not been developed as they should have been developed had they had the advantage of private capital and pri-

vate enterprise pushing out its branch lines here and there where they would bring traffic to the main line. I feel that the policy of this Government in rushing into public ownership will have the same disastrous effect upon the great prairie provinces as the ownership and operation of the Intercolonial railway has had upon the Maritime Provinces.
I notice also that the Government have changed their ideas as to the powers that they have under the Order in Council passed under the War Measures Act. I have in mind that in 1917, on a trade measure, the reciprocity in wheat, hon. gentlemen who are now members of the Government criticised that Order in Council, claiming that it was illegal, and stating that when peace came the Order in Council would cease to have effect. Those gentlemen are now members of the Government,, and apparently they have convinced the Minister of Finance-who was then certain that under the War Measures Act he had all the powers necessary to enact the reciprocity measure, and that the same authority that enabled him to pass the Order in Council, made it law just the same as an Act of Parliament-that his views were wrong, because he now comes before Parliament to ratify this Order in Council.
The hon. member for Kingston (Mr. Nickle), who has argued in favour of public ownership, has told us that if we cannot find in Canada men capable of making Government ownership of railways profitable, we shall go down to the United States. The hon. gentleman, who is a student, has surely not forgotten the experience of the United States during the past ' year. That experience was pointed out by the hon. member for East Algoma (Mr. G.
B. Nicholson) who made his speech against public ownership, but wound up by declaring himself in favour of it. Government railway operation in the United States has been disastrous to the people of that country. The whole system broke down last year in the transportation of coal. It has cost the people, as was pointed out by the hon. member for East Algoma, $150,000,000 of a deficit in operation, notwithstanding the freight rates which cost the people of that country almost $1,000,000,000. Therefore, the Government should go very carefully in their policy of Government ownership. It may be that Government ownership suits a certain section of this country, but the issues are clean cut. It is not a question of taking over the Grand Trunk Pacific; it is a ques-

tion of gradually approaching the nationalization of railways. If I stand alone upon this question-and it is not a party question on this side of the House- I am opposed to public ownership and operation of railways, because I believe it is not the best thing for this country.

As one who has taken a great deal of interest in the railway situation and transportation generally, I followed very closely the Minister of Finance (Sir Thomas White) in his admirable speech this afternoon when he laid this matter before us and showed, us exactly the position of affairs. It is certainly one that causes every thinking man to use the best powers he has to decide what it is best in the interest of this country to do at the present time. I have had the pleasure of hearing only two hon. gentlemen opposite express their views, and neither of them has made it at all clear to me what the-y would do in the situation. Our good friend, the hon. member for Chateauguay-Huntingdon (Mr. Robb), who is an excellent business man, has not told us what he proposes to do with regard to the Grand Trunk's failure to meet its obligations. The hon. member for Pontiac (Mr. Cahill) tells us that if this action was to be taken at all, it should have been taken long ago. He tells us that when the Grand Trunk failed to take over the Transcontinental and carry out the arangements, then was the time for the Government to step in, and I am rather inclined to think that is the best remark and the best criticism he made. The Government would, at that moment, have been justified in stepping in and telling the Grand Trunk management straight: You are under an obligation from which you cannot be relieved, and unless you live up to it we propose to take over the road and your shareholders will suffer accordingly. That is business. It may be hard-hearted, but in order to be just to the people of this country we sometimes have to be a little hard-hearted. And I am not sure if the Acting Prime Minister has not a little more tenderness of heart than he ought to have towards the Grand Trunk, which we all love so much.
I remember very'well hearing about the Grand Trunk since I was a child. I think it came into existence about the time I was born-I trust hon. members will not look up the date, or they will know how old I am. It is an object of affection to me. The Grand Trunk has done a great deal for Canada. T am only sorry that the company has run its head into a noose with its eyes
wide open and finds that it cannot now get out, and this country cannot afford to let it out. The hon. member for South York (Mr. W. F. Maclean), I think said that we were going to get hold of a going concern. I think we may go further and say that we are going to get hold of a coming concern, by the look of it. I cannot see that anything else is possible. The Grand Trunk have undertaken obligations amounting to $125,000,000 or $150,000,000 with their eyes wide open. They have induced this country to put in two or three hunderd million dollars that never should have been put in. .Do not say that I am a prophet after the event. I opposed that with all my might in 1903 and 1904. I fought it to a finish in that election and finally won out on that issue alone, namely, that it was a monstrous burden to put on the shoulders of the people of Canada. I said that it was a gigantic white elephant that would eat hay day and night if we are not careful, and that is what has happened since then. In the first place, the railway was built far in advance of its time. Everybody knows that Canada cannot reasonably support three transcontinental railways. I do not think it is possible to make them pay; and even if the suggestion of my good friend the hon. member for East Algoma (Mr. G. B. Nicholson) were carried out and the capital were reduced to one-half, I doubt if it could be made a success on that basis, because it is far in advance of its time and it may not pay even for the running. But the Government was forced to take action. The Grand Trunk gave notice that on a certain date they would cease operations. What would one do in such a case? Several thousands of miles of railway are going to come to a standstill and hundreds of millions of dollars of the people's money are invested in them. Are you going to allow that road to cease operation? Are you going to allow all the freight to be thrown out and the passengers to go afoot? Such a condition of affairs could not be thought of. This Government was forced to take action. I find fault with my hon. friend (Mr. Robb) that he did not tell the Government what they ought to do. One gentleman says that the Government did not take action early enough; the other one apparently is blaming the Government for taking the action now. In my judgment the Government should have taken action in the first place. That was business. But the Government wanted to be lenient, and it often happens that leniency is interpreted into one's being a

dead easy mark. That is apparently what the Grand Trunk thought. They thought that this Government was a dead easy mark, and that as they had unloaded 1,000 miles of comparatively worthless railway on to them, it would be just as easy to unload 1,500 or 2,000 miles in the same way and slip from their obligations, and apparently forget all about it,, because, in a letter which the Acting Prime Minister (Sir Thomas White) read this afternoon, the Grand Trunk Eailway forget altogether that their name is on this paper. They are calmly oblivious of the fact that they have obligated themselves to pay to this country, in round figures, $125,000,000 to $150,000,000. I, for one, am not at all disposed to let the Grand Trunk out. I agree that they helped this country at a time when it sorely needed assistance; but they, as a corporation, have undertaken obligations that they now, in an honourable way, as business men, are called upon to carry out. Unfortunately the shareholders are over the water, and, as too often happens, they may think, because they do not know the facts, that we are acting unjustly. I think this country has been most remarkably lenient with the Grand Trunk. We have delayed too long. I am only sorry that the action has to be taken now when the tremendous financial burdens of the war are confronting the Minister of Finance. I am sorry for him and for the country. I am, in a large measure, in favour of the nationalization of railways; and in spite of the fact that it has not paid in some countries, I believe they may be made to pay in Canada. I am sorry, however, that this Grand Trunk question has come up at this moment when we are submerged by financial obligations in other directions. But it had to be faced because the wheels of commerce were slowing, and this Government has, I think, at last taken heroic steps to meet the situation.
I do not know whether they have fully observed one fact, and I want to call special attention of the minister to it, namely, that the Grand Trunk, which may possibly come into our hands sooner or later, has a large mileage in the United States. Both its eastern and its western terminals are in the United States, beginning at Chicago and ending at Portland, Maine. I do not know whether the Dominion Government .is competent to run railways in the United States. Probably the Government has looked into the matter. I have not heard the minister make a Statement in reference to the question, but it is one that is worth while lookin? into.
[;Mr. Cockshutt.]
Will the United States allow the Canadian Government to run railways within their borders just the same as they would a private corporation, or will the Canadian Government be under some special obligation that a private corporation would not be under? Is it necessary to take out special charters under which those lines may be operated? There is also the question of the Port at Portland and the terminals at Chicago which have to be dealt with. I think that is a very important matter and that it must not be overlooked in the taking over of the Grand Trunk Eailway Company.
There are branches of the Canadian Northern in the United States.

I do not think there
are many branches there. There are thirty or forty miles of road running through the corner of Minnesota, but it is a very different proposition from the Grand Trunk.
It is the same principle.

That may be, but
our Government was not running the Transcontinental until very recently: I do not know whether they have struck any snags with regard to it. I am pointing out that I did not hear the minister say anything with regard to that phase, and I hope the matter has not been overlooked because it is of great importance. The hon. member for Al-gom-a (Mr. Nicholson) has given us some very interesting figures, as he did last year. He is a new member, but I think he has put on Hansard the best exposition of the railway situation given by any man in the House, bar none. I am not speaking of his speech to-night so much as the one he made a year laigo in this House. I have perused it often and he certainly put on Hansard an enormous amount of material. I do not know whether he prepared them all himself, but if he did he is certainly an encyclopedia on figures. Be that as it may, as he stated to-night, the figures have stood the test of time. I have not heard a single hon. member endeavour to prove incorrect the figures he gave. His speech last year was very valuable, and if any hon. member has not read it and desires to be seized of the railway situation in Canada, he could not do better than read that speech because it hits the situation off admirably.
One point I have not heard mentioned, to-night is the earning powers of the railways per mile and I think that is important. I see by page xii of the Drayton-Acworth report that the old Grand Trunk is earning more per mile than

any other road in Canada, its earnings being $10,983 per mile. That is a very respectable earning, but unfortunately, as so often happens, there is something else to be taken into acoount which makes the road one of the poorest paying railways, instead of one of the better paying railways, and that information is given on the bottom of the same page. It shows that the Canadian Pacific cost in round numbers $68,000 per mile, the Canadian Northern $44,000 per miile, and the old Grand Trunk $127,000 per mile. The Grand Trunk was built in prewar times when everything was supposed to be mighty cheap, and yet it cost more than double either of the other roads.

They must have
charged a large amount to capital which should have been charged to maintenance.
They have not so many hills in the United States.

They have a good many mountains. They cross the Rockies, and they are pretty hard to cross. They do things in the United States on a quicker basis. That was well illustrated during the war. I remember the Prime Minister of



Canada (Sir Robert Borden) telling a story in the House with regard to what Canada had done in the building of railways at the front. When he came back from the front two years ago he said that after Vimy Ridge was taken a certain piece of railway had to be built. The British railway experts were asked to look over the ground and say how long It would take them to do the work, as it was wanted in a great hurry. They said it would take six weeks to build that road. The British generals shook their heads and said "That is no use to us. We must have something better than that." And some one told them to get Captain Jack Stewart. He was sent for, and came and looked over the ground and said: "Give me two battalions of railway construction men and I will build the road for you in a week." They took him on, and what did he do? He had the road all built in four days. That is on Hansard, and was put there by the first Minister of Canada. Therefore I say that we know how to railroad in both Canada and the United States. We know how to build; we can build as quickly and as cheaply as any nation in the world. I am firmly convinced of that. We have the class of men that can do it, but we must secure them. I am not sure that we have all that we should have in the Commission to run all the railroads the Government purposes taking over, but I think the Government are well advised in taking this step; and if they are to be criticised they are to be criticised for being slow, not for being too fast. They have been long-suffering with the Grand Trunk. In my judgment these people have been defaulters for the past two years. It is a strong term to use, but the moment they said that they did not propose to carry out their agreement with regard to the ...Transcontinental, I think they broke their agreement absolutely, and every business man, I believe, will say so. This is the second time, and apparently they thought their bluff would work. Fortunately the War Measures Act was there. I think it is the salvation of the whole situation. I do not think the Grand Trunk expected what has happened, but they are up against it, and we have to see it through, and that money has to be raised to do it. As I said, I am sorry it has come at this time, but, I, for one, am willing to support the Finance Minister in this matter, and I think we can be defended in the country, and that the people of Canada, once they realize its absolute necessity, will say, " The Government has done wisely. Go ahead and win out and we are with you," and will help all [Mr. Cocksliutt.1
we can to make the great natioftal enterprise of Canada in the railway business that success that I feel sure it ought to be, and can be, if managed properly by the right men.

I want to say a few words along some new lines. I really consider that the action that the Government has taken, and has been taking, in this matter involves some of the most serious questions that to-day confront Canada -questions far more serious than repatriation, remobilization or reconstruction. Far more serious than any of these things is the present railway situation in Canada. I desire to draw your attention to the fact that the Canadian Government railroads have adopted the McAdoo scale of wages and time limit, with the result that some of the conductors on the railroads to-day are getting $5,000 a year, and the highest-paid workers in all Canada to-day are the railroad employees. The railroad runs from the Atlantic to the Pacific, with hundreds of thousands of employees, all of whom are bound together in one solid brotherhood; and when you adopt a rate of wages borrowed from a politician in the United States who is looking for the Presidential nomination, and give that rate to our railway employees, is it not obvious that you have produced, not a military despotism but a railroad despotism which will be a chain around the neck of fair Canada and will drag her to her grave unless you are extremely careful? How will you lower the wages of these men? They are linked together in one great brotherhood, and can hold up the whole railway system and can make any government get down on its knees within half an hour. It seems to me it must follow that all wages must go up proportionately, and I think the high cost of living will have to be maintained on that basis, because these things follow one another from mathematical necessity; and so long as that condition of things obtains, just so long will the high cost of living continue. The cost of transportation has doubled, and in some cases more than doubled. That may be very well in war time but how is it to be remedied in peace time when you have produced such a purely artificial condition of things? As I said last session, I am personally in favour of government ownership of railroads provided they can be managed the same as private corporations. The question whether government ownership is good or bad all depends on the management, and that is one of the most serious problems in connection with

the ownership of railroads. Indeed, I think it is the most serious question before the country to-day. We have suffered very much from our government railroad system in the province of Prince Edward Island. Our province has sold itself body and soul; it has sold its birthright for a mess of pottage, a narrow-gauge railroad, as crooked as a ram's horn. However, that does not enter into this question. The whole question is, how are you going to overcome the difficulties confronting this Government, or any other government, with regard to the adoption of the McAdoo scale of wages? A man who is representing a constituency through which a railroad under this system runs, should he dare open his mouth,-as I am doing to-night,-and call the attention of the public to the danger of the situation, is apt to be roughly handled by these railroad employees when he goes to the country again. It is only one man . in a thousand who will dare open his mouth if the railroad goes through his constituency. However, I have a public duty to perform, and I do not care very much whether I come back or not. If I have to run, I will take my chance and will " hew to the line, let the chips fall where they may."

I do not know anything about the legal aspect of the question, but I do not see how the Government could do anything else, from a business standpoint, than pass the resolution. Whether, from a legal standpoint we are in a good position or not, I am not prepared to say. As a matter of fact, the Grand Trunk, I understand, did not default. Therefore, that puts them, I should think, in a better position than otherwise they would be in. As to the future of the Grand Trunk, the only question, to my mind, is whether it would be cheaper and better in the interests of the country, owing to the position in which the Grand Trunk finds itself, to make a contract with them to deliver freight to our Transcontinental road on a certain basis, or whether it would be cheaper for us to operate the road ourselves. These lines run all through the northern, central and southern parts of Ontario. They are able to feed the transcontinental railways whether they be the Canadian Pacific or the Government Railway, and give them very good service. Many of these branches of the Grand Trunk are not paying, and cannot be made tp pay within any man's lifetime. Whether it would be wise for us to operate these roads in face of the fact that they cannot be made to pay, or whether
it would be better for us, now that we are in possession of the Grand Trunk Pacific, to make a traffic arrangement whereby they should deliver freight to us for the long haul, is a question for this House to decide.
The legislation does not propose to take over the old Grand Trunk. It proposes to take over and operate the Grand Trunk Pacific. I do not see, from a business standpoint, what else the Government can do. My hon. friend from Brantford (Mr. Cockshuitt) spoke about the cost of the Grand Trunk. The Grand Trunk cost more than any other railway because it was built through the Canadian wilderness. They had to carry their supplies at an enormous cost by ox teams and other means of transportation. The old Great Western Railway, now part of the Grand Trunk, had to be chopped through the country that it traversed. I do not wonder that it cost more than it would in modern times because in modern times in building railways you have the benefit of the railways in existence, to a certain extent, to haul your supplies.
With reference to the Canadian National Railways, it is absurd to have so many men on the directorate, and it is equally absurd to appoint men who know nothing about railways, no matter what their other business experience has been. My experience has taught me that if you have been brought up in a certain line of business and you go into another line of business you know nothing about, and invest in it, you are liable to lose your money. There is nobody who is capable of doing everything, and the man who makes a success in one line of business, whether it be farming, manufacturing, or merchandising, deserves success because competition is very keen. Why you appoint men as directors of these roads who know nothing about railroading is more than I can comprehend. It is not what the late Government promised us when the Canadian Northern Railway was taken over. I think the directorate of the Government road should be dependent upon Parliament itself. The directors should be chosen regardless of price from amongst capable railway men who know their business. If the Government own the railways, if they cut out all duplications, especially duplications of terminals, and run them from a practical business standpoint, there is no reason on earth why the transportation system of this country should not be made to pay.
With reference to the statement that the government operation of railways in Eng-

land has been made to pay, we read in the paper the other day that it had not paid during the war. Yet the railways in England were conducted on the very best possible basis. They appointed the managers of all the great railways in England to operate them during the war. We 'know that the German system of railways paid but they paid much lower wages and they charged twice as much for transportation. Some person said to-night that we had in Canada cheaper transportation than any country in the world except the United States. And he might as well have said, " including the Uniter! States."
In so far as the operation of the railways by the Government of the United States is concerned, anybody who has travelled since the taking over of the railways in the last two or three years knows that the accommodation given to the public is nothing like it was before. The inconvenience to the public is disgraceful on many of the roads in the United States. There never was such a glut in freight. I do not blame them for that because it was an exceptional time, the weather was very severe and there were some things that went against them. But the United States Congress voted a revolving credit of ,$500,000,000 and recently they asked for another 1750,000,000 revolving credit. They did not get it. They owe in rentals on the properties taken over something in the neighbourhood of 3700,000,000. That would not, in my judgment, be an argument against the Government operation of railways in the United States. Had they been operated by a man who understood the business there might have been a better showing. No matter how good a Secretary of the Treasury Mr. MacAdoo may be, he did not know anything about the operation of railways. He thought he did. He is just another of those men in this world who think they know something about everything and who try to make a success of some business other than their own but end up by making a failure. It all comes back to the same principle; if we are going to operate railways, we must operate them on business principles and we must have men who understand their business practically regardless of price. If we do not follow that plan we will not make a success of them. The reason I got up was to suggest that we might find it cheaper, in place of taking over the old Grand Trunk, to make a running arrangement with them, whereby they would feed our railways, and 
do it cheaper than we could feed them ourselves.
Mr. JEAN J. DENIS (Joliette):	Mr. Chairman, I have heard hon. members on the other side of the House say that no practical proposition or plan had been suggested on this side of the House as to what should be done. I will take the liberty of giving my humble opinion to the Government as to the policy that should be pursued.
Now, I am considering this as a mere business proposition, and regarding the Grand Trunk Bailway proper, and the Grand Trunk Pacific Bailway as individuals who have contracts with the Government. Here we find three parties to a contract or obligation. One party is the Grand Trunk proper. The Grand Trunk proper has assumed the responsibility of running the Grand Trunk Pacific according to a contract, or a lease which has been referred to and sufficiently explained. Suddenly the Grand Trunk Bailway fails to fulfill its obligations, and serves a notice to that effect upon the Government, just as a man who signs a note at the bank advises the institution three days before the note matures that on the date fixed for its payment he will be unable to meet the obligation. Under the circumstances the bank would be justified in taking all necessary means to protect its interests, and this is what the Government has been doing in the present situation. Because the interest of the Government in this matter is twofold. One is the general interest of the country;- the Government owes it to the country to see that these roads continue to run, because that is absolutely necessary; the soundness of this everyone will admit. The other interest which the Government has in this matter is a pecuniary one, because it has endorsed the notes of the Grand Trunk and Grand Trunk Pacific Bailways. One of the parties serves notice- upon the Government that he is not going to fulfill his part of the agreement, and at once the Government take advantage of the War Measures Act and puts this railroad into the hands of a receiver. To my mind, there was nothing else it could do. However, this is not a solution of the problem, and all that we have heard so far has been a plea on the part of the Acting Prime Minister that the Government acted properly in placing this road in a receiver's hands. For the time being, I quite understand, the Government had to face a situation which could not be delayed, a situation of urgency, and it took control of the railway. So far I am satisfied with the stand that the Govern-

ment has taken. But what is it going to do with the railway, now that it is in possession of it? I have one suggestion to make. In my opinion the Government should go direct to the Grand Trunk Railway Company and tell it: We will give you so much time to fulfill your obligations; if you do not do so, if you have a white elephant on your hands, you need not expect that the Government will relieve you of it; if you entered into a bad business proposition, that is no reason why the Government should relieve you of the responsibility; the Grand Trunk Railway Company has got to discharge its obligations and should be called upon to do so; if it does not do so then it must assume the responsibility and will be held strictly accountable for it.
Now, there is a way of doing that. The Government has a mortgage on the Grand Trunk Railway properties for the money which the Grand Trunk owes to it. Very well, the Government will act in the same way, as an individual does towards another person who owes him money and does not pay it. The Government will take control of the road and then it will have the two railways, and it will be a bad proposition for it because the Government cannot make money out of operating railroads. It may be a bad proposition for the time being, and this leads me to the point which was argued at length by the hon. member for Kingston (Mr. Nickle), viz: Is it a good or a bad policy for the Government to own and administer railroads? I do not think it is a good proposition for any Government to own railroads when it can avoid doing so. If it cannot avoid it, but is forced to assume the ownership and operation, it must continue to administer and own them until it can dispose of them. If, later on, it transpires that the Government, in some way or another, can dispose of these roads, then so much the better for the country, because I do not think that that Government will ever make any money out of Government ownership of these railways. If the Government cannot avoid doing otherwise, it is better for it to take hold of the Grand Trunk Railway now, than to assume control of that railway in one or two years. It would have been better for the Government not to have loaned money, not to have guaranteed the loans of the Grand Trunk and Grand Trunk Pacific Railway, as it has been doing, for the last three or four years, or perhaps longer. When the Government found out a year ago, or two or three years ago, that these railways could not be successfully operated, and that it was only a question of time before they would pass
into the receiver's hands, I think it should have taken the pill then and saved the money which has been expended in the period which has elapsed since that time. Every one admits, )I believe, that the Grand Trunk Railway will never be able to meet its obligations. If the Government is now convinced that it will not be able to do so, then it should take control of the Grand Trunk as well as the Grand Trunk Pacific;, it will lose less money by taking control of the road now than it will do in a few years from now.
The Acting Prime Minister told us this afternoon that the Government wanted to* be lenient towards the Grand Trunk, and not exact what he called " the pound of flesh." I do not think that is proper. Tins' is a business proposition, and the Acting Prime Minister, no more than any one else in the Government, has any right to give up one dollar of the people's money. If the Grand Trunk Railway Company owes money to this country it should pay every dollar of it. That is my contention. The Government and the country is sufficiently in need of money to warrant the collection of every cent that is owing to Canada.
At any rate what are we going to do now? The Government has a deficit of $100,000,000 a year, taking the financial situation as it now stands. We have to tax the people of this country in order to meet our obligations by means of an Income Tax, which is equivalent to taking money out of the people's pockets directly. However, no one will blame the Government for doing so because it is an unavoidable procedure. We are not in a position to give anybody a present. It is the duty of the Government to force the Grand Trunk to fulfil its obligations to the letter. If the Grand Grand Trunk cannot fulfil its obligations, then let the Government take possession of the system and do now what will be even more difficult to do a year or two hence if this matter is delayed.

On February 28, 1919, the Prime Minister was informed that the Grand Trunk Railway Company did not intend to carry on the operations of the Grand Trunk Pacific after the tenth of March. There must have been some previous conversations or correspondence between the officials of the Grand Trunk Railway Company and the Government, and before the Government is compelled to take over the Grand Trunk Pacific Railway system without giving the matter further consideration, I think the Acting Prime Minister should tell us, if

he is in a position to do so, what conversations took place and what correspondence was exchanged between the officials of the Grand Trunk Railway Company and the Government.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I placed that information on Hansard the other day when I made my statement to the House respecting the passing of the Order in Council.

What has been placed on Hansard is not exactly what I want. The letter which my hon. friend read must have followed correspondence, or at least conversations, between representatives of the Government and officials of the company.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
I understood my hon. friend to refer to the letter of March 4, in which the Government was notified by the president of the Grand Trunk Railway Company that, in view of the fact that the increased rates applicable to the Grand Trunk Pacific Railway had not been sufficient to meet the increased operating expenses, it would not be possible for the company to continue its operations when the present funds had been exhausted, which would be about the 10th instant. There had been no conversations relating to the cessation of operation of the Grand Trunk Pacific Railway Company, and in my cable to Mr. Smithers, which I presented to the House, I stated that this notification was of a peremptory character, without previous intimation or discussion. To show my hon. friend that there would have been no use in attempting negotiations with the Grand Trunk Pacific Railway Company, unless the Government decided to change its opinion and decision and to make further advances to the company, I wish to read the following cable from Mr. Smithers, dated March 11, 1919, in reply to the message which I had sent to him:
In reply to your message I assure you nothing peremptory was intended. Government having taken position in message received here March 3rd that they would not render further assistance and Grand Trunk Pacific working cash being exhausted owing to heavily increased expenses beyond power of company to control, we had no alternative but to notify Government of our inability to continue in order to prevent inconvenience to the people of Canada served by Grand Trunk Pacific. Special general meeting of Grand Trunk Railway Company has been called for Friday, 21st.
I place that on Hansard in order to give my hon. friend all the information we have respecting the matter.

speakeroldname: Mr. McKENZIE (Cape Breton North and Victoria) :
speechtext:
Is it the intention of the Govern-

ment to assume all the liabilities of this road?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: The position of the Government is that of receiver. The Government is not assuming the responsibilities of the Grand Trunk Pacific. Application will be made by the Government to the Exchequer Court for the issue of a receiver's certificate to meet any deficit in operating expenses, and the Government will, of course, be obliged to meet the interest upon Grand Trunk Pacific securities which it has guaranteed. 'But with regard to other securities, its position is merely that of receiver.

When the Government took over the Canadian Northern they took also all its liabilities and paid for the equity of redemption, some 110,000,000. I cannot see much difference between the Canadian Northern Railway Company then and the Grand Trunk Pacific Railway Company in this case. In the former case the Government established a certain precedent, and I wanted to know whether the Government intended to follow that precedent in this case.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: What I understood my hon. friend to suggest was that the Dominion Government, instead of being merely receiver, should assume all the liabilities of the Grand Trunk Pacific, and relieve the Grand Trunk Railway Company of them entirely.

Oh, no. When the Government takes possession of this property nolens volens unless they get clear of it by an Act of Parliament they are responsible, as a matter of law, to the owner of these securities.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
I do not concur in my hon. friend's view. The Dominion Government is receiver under an Order in Council which has the effect of a statute or an order of the court; and a receiver is not responsible for the liabilities of a company. The position of receiver appointed by a court is that of a custodian to continue the operation of a business subject to and pending further orders of the court from time to time. This legislation makes the Minister of Railways the receiver in this case, with the duties and the powers attaching to that office. The resolution defines the position of the Government in respect of the system in express terms, indicates the duties and powers of the receiver and expressly states that the Dominion Government is not liable to the Grand Trunk Railway Company or to any other

creditor. When this Order in Council is approved by Parliament it will become of the validity of an Act of Parliament, and its effect will be determined in accordance with its provisions, and not otherwise.

I quite understand the minister now. The position which I take, speaking for myself alone and not for any party, is this: I do not for one moment admit that the Government have any jurisdiction to do what they have done in this matter, unless we validate their action by Act of Parliament. The Government are simply mortgagees in possession and are in exactly the same position as a mortgagee in possession would be in without foreclosure.
If the third, fourth, or fifth, or even the first, mortgagee goes into possession without foreclosure he assumes all the encumbrances on the property. Every lawyer sitting around the Minister will admit that that is good law and unless we validate by Act of Parliament the action of the Government, I am afraid that any judge would say they had assumed the responsibility when they took over the property. For a creditor of the Company might say: Tf you had let the Company go on it would have paid off my liability, hut as you have prevented that you must pay the money that is owing to me. Of couse if there is to be legislation whereby we put ourselves in the place of a receiver and take all our instructions fiom the judge, that is a different matter. If the Government are going to put the road up to auction and will only pay what the-road brings at auction that puts it in a different light entirely. But the Minister did not in his very excellent speech this afternoon tell us that that was going to be done. If the Minister will tell this House that all the steps that a receiver would take under the orders of a court of this country are to be taken by the Minister of Railways and Canals, and that the country will only pay for this road what it brings at auction, I have no fault to find. But I do feel we had no business to step in and take hold of this property and make ourselves liable for $200,000,000 when, as hon. gentlemen have frequently told us, the property is not worth it. With the liabilities away above what the property is worth we are certainly not making any bargain.

This afternoon I drew the
minister's attention to a statement he made . with regard to branch lines, as to whether the provinces had prior rights over the Dominion. The minister promised to clear the point up and let the House know where we
should stand in regard to branch lines that are a part of this system. I think he forgot to mention that this evening.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
The position of
the Minister of Railways is receiver for the Grand Trunk Pacific Railway Company, including the branch lines. His position is not different from that of a statutory receiver, and the rights of all parties are preserved. The rights of the provinces as guarantors are preserved and remain under the several instruments or trust mortgages under which they can claim. The receiver must take his orders from the Exchequer Court. Just as the rights of all other parties are preserved, so are the rights of the Dominion Government preserved. It is open to the Dominion Government to enforce, by permission of the courts, any rights which it has as creditor, or as guarantor, or as mortgagee under the first mortgage or afterwards. There is no question as to the Receiver's position. His duty is to conserve, operate, and act under the orders of the Court. My hon. friend the leader of the Opposition this afternoon called attention to the Winding-Up Act. The Winding-Up Act concerns the liquidator. It is the duty of a liquidator to bring a business to a termination and to sell, but the duty of a receiver is to conserve, operate, and carry on.
If hon. gentlemen will observe the terms of this resolution, they will find the jurisdiction of the Exchequer Court is really-enlarged, the intention being that the operation of this railway system, being, as it is, in the national interest, shall be continued under the orders of the Court, and that in all orders which the Court shall make it shall have regard not only to property rights but to paramount national interest.

Perhaps I did not make myself clear. Is there anything to prevent the provinces which have priority rights on branch lines from foreclosing and selling the branch lines to others, thereby leaving the Grand Trunk Pacific without feeders?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
If default occurred under the terms of the mortgages securing the issues which they have guaranteed, the provinces could make application to the Exchequer Court, of which application they would have to give written notice to the minister, who would appear by counsel at the hearing. The Court in determining what should be done would take into consideration, under the terms

of this order, which will be validated by our legislation, not only the property rights involved, but the national interest. The intention of this order was to ensure the continued operation in the public interest of the Grand Trunk Pacific Railway system, and it was not possible to accomplish that in any other way than the one we have taken.

There is some further information required to complete the minister's statement. When the Grand Trunk failed to accept that portion of the line which was constructed by the Government from Moncton to Winnipeg, was any written agreement made between the Government and the Grand Trunk or the Grand Trunk Pacific?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: No.
Then was the company put in default?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: The Government claim they are in default, but the company set up various grounds on which they consider themselves not liable. In reality, the cost was so great that the objection was really on that ground. The interest at three per cent on $170,000,000 amounted to about $5,000,000 a year on a line which does not meet its operating expenses.
Was any agreement made at the time of default between the Government and the Grand Trunk or the Grand Trunk Pacific?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: No. The Government stepped in because it had built the line. The title was in the Government. The Grand Trunk Pacific having declined to execute the lease which under the original agreement we claim they were bound to execute, the Government had to provide for the operation of the line, and has been in possession since.
But as the Government did not put the company in default when they failed to take up their obligations it may have given up its right under the agreement to compel the company to do so.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
I think all rights are preserved.
Resolution reported, read the first and second time, and concurred in.
Sir THOMAS WHITE thereupon moved . for leave to introduce Bill No. 28, to confirm an order of the Governor General in Council respecting the Grand Trunk Pacific Railway system.

Motion agreed to, and Bill read the first time.
On motion of Sir Thomas White, the House adjourned at 11 p.m.
Friday, March 21, 1919.
